Rate-limited; retry fewer calls.Je n'ai pas pu consulter la bibliothèque Sefaria pour cette réponse. Elle a renvoyé une erreur « trop de requêtes » à chaque appel. Ce qui suit vient donc de ma connaissance générale de la littérature juive, et je n'ai relu aucun texte cité. Les références sont celles que je connais bien, mais je n'ai pas pu les vérifier. Je n'en donne aucune pour les passages dont je ne suis pas sûr. Je peux reprendre chaque point avec les textes exacts si vous me le demandez dans quelques instants.

Moïse (*Moshé Rabbénou*) est présent à presque toutes les époques de la littérature juive. La Torah elle-même le décrit comme le prophète sans égal, les sages en font le maître de tous les prophètes, les philosophes en font un principe de foi, et la Kabbale en fait une dimension spirituelle présente dans chaque génération.

## Points clés
- La Torah le décrit comme le plus humble des hommes et le seul prophète qui parlait à D.ieu « face à face ».
- Les sages (Mishna, Talmud, Midrash) en font le premier maillon de la chaîne de transmission de la Torah.
- Maïmonide en fait un des treize principes de foi : sa prophétie est d'un niveau unique.
- La Kabbale (Zohar, Arizal) et le hassidisme (Tanya) voient en Moïse une force spirituelle qui se prolonge dans chaque génération.
- Hors de la tradition juive, des auteurs antiques (Philon, Flavius Josèphe) et d'autres religions parlent aussi de lui.

## 1. Le texte de la Torah (le *péchat*, sens littéral)
- [Deuteronomy 34:10] dit qu'aucun prophète ne s'est levé en Israël comme Moïse, que D.ieu connaissait « face à face ».
- [Numbers 12:3] le dit « très humble, plus que tout homme sur la terre ».
- [Numbers 12:6-8] distingue sa prophétie de celle des autres prophètes. Eux reçoivent des visions et des songes, alors que lui reçoit une parole directe.
- [Exodus 33:11] dit que D.ieu parlait à Moïse « comme un homme parle à son prochain ».

## 2. Les sages (Mishna, Talmud, Midrash)
- [Pirkei Avot 1:1] ouvre la chaîne de transmission par « Moïse reçut la Torah du Sinaï ». Moïse en est donc le premier maillon, avant Josué, les Anciens et les prophètes.
- Le Talmud et le Midrash développent beaucoup sa vie : sa naissance, sa fuite, le buisson ardent, son rôle d'intercesseur après le veau d'or, et sa mort. Les passages centraux sont dans les traités Shabbat (la montée au ciel), Sotah (sa mort et son désir d'entrer en terre d'Israël) et Ménakhot (l'épisode de la classe de rabbi Akiva), ainsi que dans *Shemot Rabba* et *Devarim Rabba*. Je cite ces traités de mémoire, sans numéro de page.
- Les sages font aussi de lui le modèle du chef qui se met au service de son peuple.

## 3. Les décisionnaires et les philosophes
- Maïmonide fait de la prophétie de Moïse un principe de foi dans son commentaire sur la Mishna (introduction au chapitre *Perek Hélek* de Sanhédrin). Il y affirme que la prophétie de Moïse est d'une nature différente de celle de tous les autres prophètes.
- Dans le *Mishné Torah*, il développe cette différence dans les *Lois des fondements de la Torah*, chapitre 7. Je l'ai lu, mais le texte n'a pas pu être rechargé ici.
- Parmi les commentateurs de la Torah, Rachi, le Ramban, Ibn Ezra, le Sforno et d'autres reviennent sans cesse sur son caractère, sur ses fautes (le rocher à Mériba) et sur sa grandeur.

## 4. La Kabbale
- Dans le Zohar, Moïse est le « berger fidèle » (*Ra'ya Mehemna*). Une grande partie des sections appelées *Ra'ya Mehemna* présente un dialogue entre lui et rabbi Shimon bar Yohaï sur les commandements.
- Le Zohar et la tradition kabbalistique enseignent qu'une « extension de Moïse » (*itpashtouta de-Moshé*) existe dans chaque génération. C'est une force spirituelle présente chez les vrais chefs et les sages, qui transmet la Torah. C'est un enseignement kabbalistique, pas un sens littéral du texte.
- Les kabbalistes associent Moïse à une dimension précise des *séfirot* (les dix émanations divines). Les écoles ne s'accordent pas tout à fait, et je ne veux pas trancher de mémoire entre les attributions à *Tiféret*, à *Netsah* ou à *Da'at*.

## 5. Le hassidisme
- Le *Tanya* (Rabbi Shneour Zalman de Liadi) décrit Moïse comme le « berger de la foi » et la source de la *da'at* (connaissance profonde de D.ieu) pour Israël. Ce thème revient plusieurs fois dans la première partie, mais je n'ai pas le numéro de chapitre exact.
- Plusieurs maîtres hassidiques (par exemple la *Sefat Emet* et le *Méor Einayim*) lisent la vie de Moïse comme un chemin spirituel que chacun peut suivre à son niveau.

## 6. Les sources non juives
- Philon d'Alexandrie (*Vie de Moïse*) et Flavius Josèphe (*Antiquités juives*) parlent de lui. Les deux ont écrit au premier siècle.
- Il est aussi une figure centrale dans le christianisme et dans l'islam, où il s'appelle *Mûsâ*. C'est une réception extérieure à la tradition juive et elle diffère de sa lecture.

Votre question est très large. Pouvez-vous dire si vous cherchez plutôt la personne historique, les enseignements des sages ou la lecture kabbalistique ? Je pourrai alors reprendre chaque source avec le texte exact.

Pour toute question pratique ou de pensée personnelle, adressez-vous à votre rabbin.

answer:
זה הדיבור המתחיל השני ברש״י על התורה. רש״י פותח בדרש: העולם נברא "בשביל התורה" ו"בשביל ישראל", ששניהם נקראים "ראשית". אחר כך הוא מביא את הפשט: "בראשית ברא" הוא סמיכות, כלומר "בראשית ברוא אלוהים", והפסוק אינו מלמד איזה דבר נברא ראשון.

## נקודות מרכזיות
- לדעת רש״י, "אין המקרא הזה אומר אלא דרשני", והדרשה היא שהעולם נברא בשביל התורה ובשביל ישראל.
- לפי הפשט, "בראשית" הוא צורת סמיכות, ו"בראשית ברא" פירושו "בתחילת ברוא".
- רש״י מביא לכך הוכחות מהמקרא: "בראשית ממלכת", "ראשית ממלכתו", "ראשית דגנך", ו"תחלת דבר ה׳ בהושע".
- רש״י דוחה את הפירוש שהשמים והארץ נבראו ראשונים, והוא מוכיח שהמים קדמו להם.
- המסקנה היא שהמקרא אינו מלמד כלום על סדר המוקדמים והמאוחרים בבריאה.

## הלשון
> "בראשית ברא אֵין הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה אוֹמֵר אֶלָּא דָּרְשֵׁנִי..."

[Rashi on Genesis 1:1:2]

## א. הדרש
רש״י מביא את דרשת רבותינו: העולם נברא "בשביל התורה שנקראת ראשית דרכו" (משלי ח) ו"בשביל ישראל שנקראו ראשית תבואתו" (ירמיה ב). המילה "בראשית" נדרשת כאן כאילו כתוב "בשביל הראשית". זו דרשה ולא פשט, ורש״י עצמו מציג אותה כך כשהוא עובר אחריה ל"אם באת לפרשו כפשוטו".

## ב. הפשט: סמיכות
רש״י קובע שאין בתנ״ך "ראשית" שאינה דבוקה למילה שאחריה. הוא מביא שלוש דוגמאות:
- "בראשית ממלכת יהויקים"
- "ראשית ממלכתו"
- "ראשית דגנך"

לכן גם כאן: "בראשית ברא אלהים" הוא כמו "בראשית ברוא". הפסוק מתחיל מתחילת הבריאה, ואחרי כן "והארץ היתה תהו ובהו... ויאמר אלהים יהי אור". רש״י מוסיף ראיה לסמיכות לפועל: "תחלת דבר ה׳ בהושע", כלומר "תחילת דיבורו של הקב״ה בהושע".

הקושי שרש״י פותר: אילו בא הפסוק ללמד שהשמים והארץ נבראו ראשונים, היה לו לכתוב "בראשונה ברא את השמים".

## ג. דחיית הפירוש האחר
רש״י מעלה טענה אפשרית: "בראשית" אולי סמוך למילה חסרה, כלומר "בראשית הכל". יש לכך דוגמאות של מקראות מקוצרים:
- "כי לא סגר דלתי בטני" (איוב ג)
- "ישא את חיל דמשק" (ישעיהו ח)
- "אם יחרוש בבקרים" (עמוס ו)
- "מגיד מראשית אחרית" (ישעיהו מו)

על כך הוא משיב: "תמה על עצמך". הוא נותן שתי ראיות שהשמים והארץ לא היו הראשונים:
1. המים קדמו, שהרי נאמר "ורוח אלהים מרחפת על פני המים", והמקרא עדיין לא גילה מתי נבראו המים.
2. השמים נבראו "מאש ומים", ולכן אש ומים היו קיימים לפניהם.

על כן "לא למד המקרא סדר המוקדמים והמאוחרים כלום".

## ד. הקשר לדיבורים הסמוכים
- בדיבור הקודם, [Rashi on Genesis 1:1:1], רש״י מסביר מדוע התורה פותחת בבראשית ולא ב"החדש הזה לכם". לפי ר׳ יצחק, כדי שאם יאמרו אומות העולם לישראל "לסטים אתם" יענו ישראל שהארץ כולה של הקב״ה, והוא נתנה למי שישר בעיניו.
- בדיבור הבא, [Rashi on Genesis 1:1:3], רש״י דן בשם "אלהים" ולא "ה׳". לפי דבריו, הקב״ה תכנן בתחילה לברוא את העולם במידת הדין, ואחר כך שיתף אליה את מידת הרחמים.

אם תרצה, אפשר להמשיך להשוואה עם הרמב״ן ועם האבן עזרא על הפסוק. הם דנים בפירוש "בראשית" ובשאלת סמיכות.

answer:
Nach der traditionellen jüdischen Chronologie lebte Noach etwa **1300 Jahre vor Moses**. Zwischen Noachs Geburt (1056 nach der Erschaffung der Welt) und Moses' Geburt (2368) liegen 1312 Jahre. Zwischen der Sintflut und Moses' Geburt liegen 712 Jahre.

Die Abfrage der Texte in Sefaria ist gerade fehlgeschlagen (Fehler 429, zu viele Anfragen). Ich habe die Verse deshalb nicht live nachgeschlagen. Die Zahlen unten stammen aus meiner Kenntnis der Verse und der traditionellen Berechnung. Bitte prüfe sie bei Bedarf an den genannten Stellen.

## Key Takeaways
- Noach wurde im Jahr 1056 nach der Erschaffung der Welt geboren, Moses im Jahr 2368. Das ergibt 1312 Jahre Abstand.
- Von der Sintflut (1656) bis zu Moses' Geburt vergingen 712 Jahre.
- Noach starb 2006, also 362 Jahre vor Moses' Geburt.
- Noach erlebte noch Avraham, der damals 58 Jahre alt war.

## Die Berechnung

**Von Adam bis Noach** ([Genesis 5:3-32](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.5.3-32)): Die Summe der Zeugungsalter von Adam bis Lemech ergibt 1056 Jahre bis zu Noachs Geburt.
- Adam 130, Set 105, Enosch 90, Kenan 70, Mahalalel 65, Jered 162, Chanoch 65, Metuschelach 187, Lemech 182.
- Die Sintflut kam, als Noach 600 Jahre alt war ([Genesis 7:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.7.6)). Das war im Jahr 1656.
- Noach wurde 950 Jahre alt ([Genesis 9:29](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.9.29)). Er starb also im Jahr 2006.

**Von Noach bis Avraham** ([Genesis 11:10-26](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.11.10-26)): Die Zeugungsalter ergeben das Jahr 1948 für Avrahams Geburt.
- Arpachschad wurde 1658 geboren, zwei Jahre nach der Flut.
- Schelach 1693, Ever 1723, Peleg 1757, Re'u 1787, Serug 1819, Nachor 1849, Terach 1878.
- Avraham wurde 1948 geboren, als Terach 70 war.

**Von Avraham bis Moses:**
- Jitzchak wurde 2048 geboren und Ja'akov 2108.
- Der Auszug aus Ägypten war im Jahr 2448. Das ergibt sich aus der traditionellen Rechnung (*Seder Olam*), die 400 Jahre von Jitzchaks Geburt bis zum Auszug zählt.
- Moses war beim Auftritt vor Pharao 80 Jahre alt ([Exodus 7:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.7.7)). Er wurde also 2368 geboren.

## Die Abstände im Überblick

| Von | Bis Moses' Geburt (2368) |
|---|---|
| Noachs Geburt (1056) | 1312 Jahre |
| Sintflut (1656) | 712 Jahre |
| Noachs Tod (2006) | 362 Jahre |

Bis zum Auszug (2448) kommen jeweils 80 Jahre dazu. Die Sintflut lag dann 792 Jahre davor.

## Hinweise
- Die Zahlen folgen der klassischen rabbinischen Chronologie, auf der auch die jüdische Jahreszählung beruht. Die Angaben der Verse lassen sich aber leicht unterschiedlich zusammenrechnen. Das betrifft zum Beispiel Shems genaues Geburtsjahr und die Frage, wie alt Terach bei Avrahams Geburt war. Kleine Abweichungen im Bereich von einigen Jahren sind deshalb möglich.
- Die Dauer des Aufenthalts in Ägypten ist ein bekanntes Problem. [Exodus 12:40](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.12.40) nennt 430 Jahre. Nach der Tradition waren es 210 Jahre in Ägypten selbst, weil die 430 Jahre schon mit der Verheißung an Avraham beginnen. Auch das wirkt sich auf die Rechnung aus.
- Moderne Geschichtswissenschaft datiert Ereignisse anders. Die obige Rechnung ist die der Tora-Tradition.

Wenn du möchtest, schaue ich die Verse und die Kommentare von Raschi dazu noch einmal im Wortlaut nach.

Да, труд под названием «Нахалат Яаков» (נחלת יעקב) от Яакова Наумбурга существует. Но проверить это по Сефарии мне не удалось: поиск вернул ошибку (слишком много запросов), а само сочинение в библиотеке я не нашёл. Поэтому ниже то, что я помню, и это нужно перепроверить.

## Ключевые выводы
- Насколько я помню, «Нахалат Яаков» Яакова Наумбурга — это суперкомментарий к комментарию Раши на Тору. Это не галахический кодекс.
- Авторитет такого сочинения — в разборе слов Раши и его источников, а не в вынесении галахических решений.
- Он не входит в число поским, на которых строится практическая галаха (Рамбам, Шулхан арух, Рема, Мишна брура и т. д.).
- Название «Нахалат Яаков» носят и другие книги разных авторов, поэтому важно уточнить, о какой именно речь.

## Что я могу и чего не могу подтвердить
- **Не подтверждено:** точные годы жизни автора, место его служения и издание. Эти данные я не стал бы приводить без проверки. Так как инструменты не сработали, я не буду придумывать биографию или цитаты.
- **Суперкомментарии на Рашо** (например, «Гур Арье» Магараля, «Сифтей хахамим», «Мизрахи») ценятся как помощь в понимании Раши. Они не заменяют сам текст и не создают галахических норм.

## Как оценивать авторитет
1. **В галахе** решают Шулхан арух с комментаторами и поским вашей общины. Если «Нахалат Яаков» процитирован как довод в практическом вопросе, смотрите, на кого он ссылается и что говорят признанные поским.
2. **В толковании Торы** это может быть полезный взгляд, который стоит сопоставить с другими комментаторами Раши.
3. **Признание в традиции** обычно видно по тому, цитируют ли автора другие авторитеты и издаётся ли он в стандартных изданиях.

answer:
Retry.נראה שהשאלה היא על הטענה ששלמה המלך הבין את שפת החיות והעופות. הפסוק המפורש מדבר על כך ש"דִּבֵּר על" בעלי החיים והעופות, ולא ששמע אותם או שוחח איתם. את המסורת שהבין את לשונם מביאים מדרשים ואגדות מאוחרים יותר.

ציטטתי כאן רק את הפסוק, כי ניסיתי להביא מקורות נוספים ומערכת Sefaria לא הגיבה (שגיאת עומס). את המקורות האחרים הזכרתי מהזיכרון, ולא אימתתי אותם עכשיו.

## עיקרי הדברים
- המקור במקרא הוא [I Kings 5:13], והלשון שם היא "וַיְדַבֵּר עַל", כלומר דיבר על הנושא.
- פשט הפסוק הוא חכמת טבע: שלמה אמר דברי חכמה ומשלים על עולם הצומח והחי.
- המסורת על הבנת לשון העופות היא מדרשית ואגדית. נזכר בה למשל התרנגול בר (הוּדהוּד) במדרש על המלכה שבא ובתרגום שני למגילת אסתר.
- אין זו הלכה ואין בה עיקר אמונה, ואפשר להבין אותה כחכמה בטבעם של בעלי החיים וגם כיכולת על־טבעית.

## הפשט
בפסוק כתוב:

"וַיְדַבֵּר֙ עַל־הַבְּהֵמָ֣ה וְעַל־הָע֔וֹף וְעַל־הָרֶ֖מֶשׂ וְעַל־הַדָּגִֽים"

בתרגום: "ודיבר על הבהמה ועל העוף ועל הרמש ועל הדגים" [I Kings 5:13].

הפסוק שלפניו מונה את שלשת אלפים המשל ואת חמשת אלפים ואחד השירים שלו, ואחריו בא הפסוק על העצים, "מן הארז אשר בלבנון ועד האזוב אשר יוצא בקיר" [I Kings 5:12-13]. ההקשר הוא חכמת שלמה בתחומי הטבע: צמחים, בהמות, עופות, רמשים ודגים. מההקשר הזה עולה שהכוונה לדברי חכמה ומשל על טבעם ותכונותיהם. בפסוק עצמו אין זכר לשיחה עם בעלי החיים או להבנת קולותיהם.

## המסורת המדרשית
- **הוּדהוּד והמלכה:** המסורת על הבנת לשון העופות מופיעה בעיקר במדרשים על מלכת שבא ובתרגום שני למגילת אסתר. שם התרנגול בר משמש שליח של שלמה. את ההפניה המדויקת לא הצלחתי לאמת עכשיו.
- **הבנה אחרת:** יש מפרשים שהבינו את "וידבר על" כידיעת טבעם ותכונותיהם של בעלי החיים, ולא כהבנת "שפה". גם לגבי זה לא הצלחתי לאמת עכשיו את לשון המפרשים.

אם תרצה, אפשר לחזור לזה בהמשך ולקרוא יחד את רש"י, רד"ק, התרגום השני למגילת אסתר ומדרשים נוספים. כדאי גם לדעת אם שאלתך נוגעת לפשט, לאגדה או לעניין אחר, כמו "שיחת בעלי חיים" אצל חז"ל בכלל.

4. [I Kings 3:16]: "אָז תָּבֹאנָה שְׁתַּיִם נָשִׁים זֹנוֹת אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ", בסיפור המשפט של שלמה.

answer:
Salmo 16 es un *mijtam* (composición de David) en el que David se refugia en Dios, lo declara su "porción" y expresa confianza en que Dios lo guiará por el camino de la vida. No pude cargar el texto desde Sefaria porque devolvió un error de límite de consultas (429). Por eso la traducción siguiente es mía, hecha de memoria, y no la he cotejado con la edición de Sefaria ni con ningún comentario. [Psalms 16:1-11]

## Puntos clave
- El salmo expresa refugio y confianza total en Dios (v. 1-2).
- Rechaza la idolatría y elige a Dios como "porción de mi herencia y de mi copa" (v. 4-6).
- Tener a Dios siempre presente da seguridad y alegría (v. 8-9).
- Termina con la certeza de que Dios lo guiará por el camino de la vida (v. 10-11).

## Traducción (mía)

**1** *Mijtam* de David. Guárdame, oh Dios, porque en Ti me refugio.

**2** Dije al Eterno: "Tú eres mi Señor; no hay para mí bien fuera de Ti".

**3** En cuanto a los santos que están en la tierra y a los nobles, en ellos está todo mi deleite.

**4** Se multiplican los dolores de quienes corren tras otro dios. Yo no derramaré sus libaciones de sangre ni tomaré sus nombres en mis labios.

**5** El Eterno es la porción de mi herencia y de mi copa; Tú sustentas mi suerte.

**6** Las cuerdas de medir me cayeron en lugares placenteros; en verdad, hermosa es mi heredad.

**7** Bendeciré al Eterno, que me aconsejó; aun por las noches mis entrañas me instruyen.

**8** Pongo al Eterno delante de mí siempre; porque está a mi diestra, no vacilaré.

**9** Por eso se alegra mi corazón y se regocija mi alma; también mi carne reposará segura.

**10** Pues no abandonarás mi alma al *Sheol* (el sepulcro); no permitirás que tu fiel vea la fosa.

**11** Me darás a conocer la senda de la vida; plenitud de alegrías ante Tu presencia, delicias a Tu diestra para siempre.

## Notas
- **Versículo 2:** el hebreo es ambiguo. Puede entenderse como "dije" o como "dijiste (oh alma mía)", y la segunda mitad también admite otras lecturas. Las traducciones varían aquí.
- **Versículos 5-6:** usan el lenguaje de la herencia de la tierra, con "porción", "copa", "suerte" y "cuerdas de medir". David dice que su verdadera herencia es Dios mismo. Esto recuerda a los levitas, de quienes se dice que Dios es su herencia.
- **Versículo 7:** "mis entrañas" (literalmente "riñones") es una imagen bíblica de la conciencia interior.
- **Versículo 10:** "fosa" (*shájat*) aparece en muchas traducciones cristianas como "corrupción". La lectura judía tradicional entiende la fosa o el sepulcro, como expresión de confianza en que Dios protegerá a David de una muerte prematura.
- **Versículo 8:** "Shiviti Hashem lenegdi tamid" ("Pongo al Eterno delante de mí siempre") es una frase muy conocida. Se cita en el *Shulján Aruj* como principio fundamental de la conciencia de Dios, y se escribe en los *shiviti* que se cuelgan en las sinagogas.

Si quieres, cuando Sefaria vuelva a responder puedo traerte el texto hebreo con vocalización y los comentarios de Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra o Metzudat David. También puedo explicar el salmo versículo por versículo.

Rate limited; retry.Working again; fetching the rest.**Short answer:** They overlapped for roughly 30 years, but the Bible never says they met, corresponded, or mentioned each other. Jeremiah prophesied in Judah and Ezekiel in Babylonian exile. Neither was widely obeyed. Jeremiah was persecuted by his own people. Ezekiel was respected and consulted, but his audience mostly didn't act on what he said.

*Source note: Sefaria returned errors for most of my lookups. I could confirm only [Jeremiah 29:1] directly. The other verse references below are from memory, so please check them before relying on them.*

## Key Takeaways
- Jeremiah and Ezekiel were both priests and both warned that Jerusalem would fall, but they worked in different places: Jerusalem and Babylon.
- No verse records a personal relationship. Any connection is indirect, mainly through Jeremiah's letter to the exiles.
- Jeremiah was a hated, imprisoned minority voice at home, though kings still consulted him in secret.
- Ezekiel was an established figure among the exiles, with elders coming to him. His listeners often treated him as entertainment.
- Their messages overlap strongly, which suggests the same prophetic message was reaching both communities.

## Timeline and location
- **Jeremiah:** He began prophesying in Josiah's reign ([Jeremiah 1:2]). He stayed in Jerusalem through the destruction in 586 BCE, then went to Mizpah and was taken to Egypt ([Jeremiah 43]).
- **Ezekiel:** He was exiled with King Jehoiachin in 597 BCE. He prophesied by the Chebar river in Babylon, beginning in the fifth year of that exile ([Ezekiel 1:1-3]).

## Was there a personal relationship?
The text gives no sign of one. Neither book names the other prophet. The one clear bridge is Jeremiah's letter to the exiles:

> "וְאֵלֶּה דִּבְרֵי הַסֵּפֶר אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַח יִרְמְיָה הַנָּבִיא מִירוּשָׁלִַם אֶל־יֶתֶר זִקְנֵי הַגּוֹלָה וְאֶל־הַכֹּהֲנִים וְאֶל־הַנְּבִיאִים וְאֶל־כָּל־הָעָם…" [Jeremiah 29:1]
> "This is the text of the letter that the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the priests, the prophets, the rest of the elders of the exile community, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had exiled from Jerusalem to Babylon."

Ezekiel belonged to that community, so he was part of its audience. The letter told the exiles to settle down and build houses, and it warned against prophets promising a quick return (my recollection of [Jeremiah 29:5-9]). Ezekiel's warnings that Jerusalem would fall (e.g. [Ezekiel 4–7], [Ezekiel 12]) fit that message. Calling this "cooperation" is my inference, not something the text states.

Other parallels, which I'm noting as my own observation:
- Both were priests ([Jeremiah 1:1]; [Ezekiel 1:3]).
- Both attack false prophets ([Jeremiah 23]; [Ezekiel 13]) and bad shepherds ([Jeremiah 23]; [Ezekiel 34]).
- Both describe eating a scroll ([Jeremiah 15:16]; [Ezekiel 2:8–3:3]).
- Both speak of a renewed heart and covenant ([Jeremiah 31:31-33]; [Ezekiel 36:26]) and of individual responsibility ([Jeremiah 31:29-30]; [Ezekiel 18]).

## Standing in the community

**Jeremiah: rejected at home.**
- He was beaten and put in the stocks by the priest Pashhur ([Jeremiah 20:1-2]).
- He was nearly put to death after the Temple sermon ([Jeremiah 26]).
- He was imprisoned and thrown into a cistern ([Jeremiah 37–38]).
- Even so, King Zedekiah consulted him privately ([Jeremiah 37:17]; [Jeremiah 38:14]).
- After the fall, the Babylonians released him ([Jeremiah 39–40]).

**Ezekiel: honored but not obeyed.**
- Elders of the exile sat before him ([Ezekiel 8:1]; [Ezekiel 14:1]; [Ezekiel 20:1]).
- Late in his ministry, God tells him the people hear his words like a pleasant song but do not act on them ([Ezekiel 33:30-32]).
- His message was vindicated when a refugee brought news that the city had fallen ([Ezekiel 33:21]).

The difference makes sense given where each stood. Jeremiah's message threatened people who still held power in Jerusalem. Ezekiel spoke to people who were already displaced and were looking for an explanation.

## Rabbinic tradition
I couldn't retrieve the Talmudic and midrashic material to check it. I know of no established rabbinic tradition about a personal meeting between them. If you're interested, I can try again to look up how the Sages treat each prophet, for example Jeremiah's lineage in [Megillah 14b], and the rabbinic discussion of Ezekiel's vision in [Chagigah 13a].

answer:
Let me retry the primary texts.# Parshat Re'eh: "Patoach Tiftach" (Open, You Shall Open)

**Title: Opening a Hand Once Is Not Enough**

The Torah doesn't only say to give to the poor. It says *patoach tiftach*, "open, you shall open" [Deuteronomy 15:8]. The doubled verb teaches that giving is not a single act. It is an ongoing posture of generosity, in which the giver pays attention to the whole person and to the giver's own heart.

## Key Takeaways
- The doubled verb *patoach tiftach* means giving must be repeated, as often as the need arises (Rashi, from the Sifrei).
- The Torah sets the measure of giving by the poor person's *need* ("whatever is sufficient to meet the need"), not by the giver's comfort.
- The Ba'al HaTurim reads the doubling as "open your hand *and* your mouth": giving includes speaking kindly and protecting the recipient's dignity.
- The Or HaChaim reads the verse as a reassurance. Giving opens "hidden treasures" and costs the giver nothing in the end.

## The Verse and Its Setting

> כִּֽי־פָתֹ֧חַ תִּפְתַּ֛ח אֶת־יָדְךָ֖ ל֑וֹ וְהַעֲבֵט֙ תַּעֲבִיטֶ֔נּוּ דֵּ֚י מַחְסֹר֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יֶחְסַ֖ר לֽוֹ
> "Rather, you must open your hand and lend whatever is sufficient to meet the need." [Deuteronomy 15:8]

The verse comes right after the Torah warns against hardening your heart and closing your hand to a needy brother (my paraphrase of the preceding verses). The word *ki* ("rather") sets up a contrast. The Torah describes the temptation to shut down and then answers it: do the opposite, and open.

## Question: Why the Double Language?

Biblical Hebrew often doubles a verb for emphasis, and Ibn Ezra notes that *patoach* here is an infinitive absolute [Ibn Ezra on Deuteronomy 15:8:1]. The tradition still asks why the Torah chose this emphasis. Several answers follow.

### 1. Again and again (Rashi)
Rashi, following the Sifrei, explains that *patoach tiftach* means you must give even many times [Rashi on Deuteronomy 15:8:1]. Poverty doesn't end after one gift. Neither does the obligation.

### 2. Giving what he actually lacks (Rashi)
Rashi reads "*dei machsoro asher yechsar lo*" (whatever he lacks) expansively. Following the Sifrei and Ketubot 67b, he says it includes even a horse to ride and a servant to run before a person who was once accustomed to that. The word *lo* ("for him") even includes helping him marry [Rashi on Deuteronomy 15:8:5; Rashi on Deuteronomy 15:8:6]. The standard is the *recipient's* lived reality, not what the giver thinks is reasonable. Rashi also notes you are not obligated to make him rich [Rashi on Deuteronomy 15:8:4].

### 3. Preserving dignity (Rashi, Rabbeinu Bahya)
"*Veha'avet ta'avitenu*" means that if he doesn't want a gift, give it as a loan [Rashi on Deuteronomy 15:8:3]. Rabbeinu Bahya adds that this is done to preserve his self-respect [Rabbeinu Bahya, Devarim 15:8:1]. The point is to ease the recipient's burden without humiliating him.

### 4. Open the hand and the mouth (Ba'al HaTurim)
The Kitzur Ba'al HaTurim offers several readings of the doubled *peh*. One is:

> פתח פ"א כפולה לומר פתח לו ידך וגם פיך לשדלו בדברים
> "The letter *peh* is doubled, to say: open your hand for him, and also your mouth, to persuade him with words." [Kitzur Ba'al HaTurim on Deuteronomy 15:8:1]

Money without a kind word, or given with a scowl, is only half of what the Torah asks. He also reads it as "if he is embarrassed, bring it to his door." The giver should seek out the poor person rather than wait to be approached.

### 5. The promise (Or HaChaim)
The Or HaChaim asks what kind of reason "*ki*" gives to a hardened heart. He answers with Proverbs 11:24, "one man gives generously and winds up with more." When a person opens his hand, God "opens the gates of heavenly bounty" for him. On his reading, what you give the poor person is effectively a loan, and God repays it with interest [Or HaChaim on Deuteronomy 15:8:1]. The Kitzur Ba'al HaTurim hints at the same idea. He connects the word to the verse about the gates of your land being opened, and says that if you open your hand, the gates of heaven open for you [Kitzur Ba'al HaTurim on Deuteronomy 15:8:3].

## A Closing Thought (my own synthesis)
The commentators share one point. The command is about the *giver's inner opening* as much as the poor person's relief. A closed hand and a closed heart go together, and the Torah doesn't let us treat generosity as a single transaction.

Putting these readings together gives a practical checklist for *patoach tiftach*:
1. **Give repeatedly**, not only when it's convenient.
2. **Give according to the person's need**, not your assumptions.
3. **Give with words**, with warmth and encouragement.
4. **Give with dignity**, ideally so the recipient isn't shamed.
5. **Give with trust** that giving never leaves you poorer.

Let me try again.The last part of your question came through garbled, so I'm not sure what you meant by "released in a semi forum" or "the seventh form of hearing." I read the question as being about Eliphaz's "six troubles… in seven" in [Job 5:19]. I answer that below and note where I'm unsure. Sefaria was rate-limiting me, so I could not retrieve the commentaries and some of Job 1–2. I mark what I'm citing from memory.

**Short answer:** Eliphaz's "six… seven" is a standard Hebrew number pattern. It means "many, and even more," and the seventh is not a special kind of affliction. The list that follows reads as an ironic preview of Job's own losses. Eliphaz presents it as a promise, and it describes what has already happened to Job. That is probably the "indirect reference" you noticed. Eliphaz does not know about the heavenly challenge, so he cannot see the irony.

## Key Takeaways
- Eliphaz argues from observation and tradition that the innocent do not perish and that suffering is *musar* (discipline) from God.
- "Six… seven" is a literary idiom for totality, so the seventh is not a separate category of suffering.
- Eliphaz's promises of protection (from famine, war, the tongue, violence, and childlessness) match Job's actual losses.
- Job 5:19 says "no evil will *touch* you" (*lo yigga'*). The prologue uses the same root, *nega'*, when the Adversary asks to "touch" Job's possessions and then his body.
- The book ends by rejecting Eliphaz's theology. Job has not been punished for sin, and the friends are rebuked.

## Eliphaz's argument
- **Suffering is punishment.** Eliphaz says: "זְכׇר־נָא מִי הוּא נָקִי אָבָד וְאֵיפֹה יְשָׁרִים נִכְחָדוּ" ("Think now, what innocent ever perished? Where have the upright been destroyed?") [Job 4:7]. The next verse adds that those who "plow evil and sow mischief reap them" [Job 4:8].
- **Suffering is discipline.** In chapter 5 he softens this: "אַשְׁרֵי אֱנוֹשׁ יוֹכִחֶנּוּ אֱלוֹהַּ" ("Happy is the person whom God reproves") [Job 5:17]. He adds that God "injures, but also binds up" [Job 5:18]. For Eliphaz, Job's pain is a call to repent, and healing will follow.
- **He knows nothing of the prologue.** The reader knows from [Job 1] and [Job 2] that the suffering follows God's praise of Job and the Adversary's challenge. The Adversary is *ha-satan*, "the accuser." In the Jewish reading he acts within God's authority, as a prosecutor in the heavenly court. He is not an independent power. Eliphaz is arguing from inside a world in which no such test exists. (I could not retrieve Job 1:8–12 this session, so I am relying on my knowledge of the text.)

## "In six troubles… in seven"
The verse reads: "בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא־יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע" ("You will be delivered from six troubles; in seven no harm will reach you") [Job 5:19].

- **The idiom.** A "three… four" or "six… seven" pattern is a known biblical device. Proverbs 6:16 and Amos 1:3 use it. It means a full and sufficient number, and the extra number marks completeness. This is my own general observation, not something I retrieved here. So the "seventh" is not a different kind of suffering. It is the point where Eliphaz claims that even the worst case will not hurt the righteous.
- **The list that follows.** Verses 20–25 give the details: famine and war [Job 5:20], "the scourging tongue" and violence [Job 5:21], wild beasts [Job 5:22–23], a peaceful tent [Job 5:24], and many descendants [Job 5:25]. He ends with a long and full life [Job 5:26].

## Why this speaks to Job's dilemma
Set against the story, almost every item on Eliphaz's list is something Job has lost or will lose:
- **Violence and plunder.** Job's flocks and servants are lost to raiders (the prologue, [Job 1]).
- **A peaceful tent and many descendants.** Job's children die when the house collapses, so he loses what Eliphaz promises the righteous will keep.
- **The scourging tongue.** Job's wife and his friends' speeches become the "tongue" that wounds him.
- **A full lifespan.** Job's children die young, the opposite of Eliphaz's image of grain gathered "in its season" [Job 5:26].

Eliphaz therefore describes an ideal that Job's life contradicts. This is my reading, not a quoted commentator's. The word "touch" strengthens it. Eliphaz says no evil will *touch* (*yigga'*) the righteous in the seventh trouble. In the prologue the Adversary asks God to "send out Your hand and *touch*" (*u-ga'*) Job's property, and later his bone and flesh. This is from memory of [Job 1:11] and [Job 2:5]. Job is touched in exactly the way Eliphaz says the righteous cannot be.

## How the book answers Eliphaz
The book does not accept Eliphaz's formula. In my recollection, God says at the end that the friends "have not spoken rightly" about Him, as Job has [Job 42:7]. I did not retrieve that verse here. Job's suffering is not the punishment Eliphaz assumes. Whether it is a test or something beyond human explanation is debated among commentators, which I did not research here.

## Please clarify
Could you restate the last part of your question? Did you mean something like "is the seventh the form of Job's *release*" or "is it the *hearing* (a trial, or God hearing him)?" If you tell me, I can look at it with the classic commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudot, Malbim) once Sefaria is available again.

answer:
# The Ark Is a Word: A Crazy Dvar Torah on Parashat Noach

Noah's ark is a *teivah*, and *teivah* also means "word." One well-known chassidic reading says God told Noah to enter a word and let it carry him through the flood. In this reading, the ark is a lesson about how to survive when the world is flooding.

**A note on sources:** Sefaria was rate-limited while I prepared this. I could retrieve and verify only [Genesis 6:14-16]. The other verses and the Baal Shem Tov tradition below come from my memory, so please check them before you use them publicly. I have marked my own creative connections as mine.

## Key Takeaways
- The Hebrew *teivah* means both "ark" and "word."
- The ark in [Genesis 6:14-16] has no steering, no sails and no rudder. It has only a skylight, a side door and three decks.
- A chassidic tradition, usually attributed to the Baal Shem Tov, reads "enter the *teivah*" as "enter the words" of prayer and Torah.
- The next parasha shows the opposite use of words: Babel's builders use them to climb, and Noah uses a word to be carried.

## 1. The strange ship

Here is the plain text of God's instructions:

> עֲשֵׂה לְךָ תֵּבַת עֲצֵי־גֹפֶר קִנִּים תַּעֲשֶׂה אֶת־הַתֵּבָה וְכָפַרְתָּ אֹתָהּ מִבַּיִת וּמִחוּץ בַּכֹּפֶר
> "Make yourself an ark of gopher wood; make it an ark with compartments, and cover it inside and out with pitch." [Genesis 6:14]

Read it as an engineer would. The ark is 300 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high. It has a *tzohar* (an opening for light, or a window), "terminate it within a cubit of the top." It has an entrance in its side and three decks [Genesis 6:15-16].

The text says nothing about a mast, oars, a rudder or a destination. Noah is not a captain. He is cargo, and the ark's whole job is to be a sealed space that holds him while everything else is water.

## 2. One word, two meanings

The Torah does not use the usual Hebrew word for a ship. It uses *teivah*, which in later Hebrew also means "word."

The only other *teivah* in the Torah is the little basket of reeds in which baby Moses is placed on the Nile ([Exodus 2:3], from memory). Both are small, enclosed vessels that save a life from water.

The Baal Shem Tov is traditionally quoted as reading God's command *"bo el ha-teivah"* ("come into the ark") as "come into the word." The floodwaters are the overwhelming pressures of the world. When they rise, don't try to out-swim them. Enter the words of Torah and prayer, and let each letter be your wall and your ceiling.

## 3. Details that fit (my own connections)

- **Pitch inside and outside.** The verb *v'chafarta* ("cover with pitch") shares a root with *kapparah*, atonement. I read this as saying that a word becomes protective when it is sealed from within and without. What you say and what you mean should match.
- **The skylight.** The *tzohar* sits at the top, so the only view is upward. In the ark you can't watch the destruction below. You can only look up. (Whether the *tzohar* was a window or a gem is a classic dispute among the early commentators. I couldn't re-check it today.)
- **The side door.** You enter a word sideways, with humility, not by storming it from the front.
- **The three decks.** I'll offer this as an image. Three levels may suggest that a word has a body (sound), a mind (meaning) and a depth (intention). Prayer lives on all three.

## 4. The twist: Babel

Next, the Torah says humanity had "one language and uniform words" ([Genesis 11:1], from memory) and used them to build a tower to the heavens.

Noah and the builders both use a structure made of materials and words. Noah's structure has a door, a skylight and no navigation. It is built to hold him. The tower is built to make a name for its builders and to climb. One generation uses words to be carried, and the other uses words to reach.

## The message

Sometimes you can't steer. The flood may be an illness, a loss, a news cycle or your own anxiety. Noah's survival doesn't come from steering. It comes from entering something sealed and holy, closing the door, and keeping his eyes on the skylight.

So pick a word this week, such as a line of *Shema*, a psalm or a blessing. Climb inside it and stay there until the water goes down.

Let me retry the ones that failed.Genesis 1:1, *Bereshit bara Elohim et ha-shamayim ve-et ha-aretz*, is usually translated "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." It says that the world has a Creator and that everything began by His will. Rashi reads the plain meaning more precisely: "At the beginning of God's creating heaven and earth…". On that reading the verse opens the story and does not state what was made first.

I couldn't retrieve the verse text itself from Sefaria, which was rate-limiting requests, so I give the verse from memory. I did retrieve Rashi and Ramban. I couldn't retrieve Ibn Ezra or Bereshit Rabbah, so I don't quote them here.

## Key Takeaways
- The verse's basic message is that God is the source of all existence and created the world by His will.
- *Bereshit* ("in the beginning") is a "construct" form. Rashi concludes that the verse means "at the beginning of God's creating" and does not teach the order of creation.
- Rashi says the verse "calls out for interpretation" (*darsheini*). Rabbinic tradition reads *reshit* as referring to the Torah and to Israel.
- Rashi, quoting Rabbi Yitzchak, says the Torah opens with creation to establish that the whole earth is God's to give to whomever He wishes.
- Ramban says the verse is the root of faith, and that the detailed workings of creation (*Ma'aseh Bereshit*) are a deep mystery.

## The plain meaning (pshat) according to Rashi
Rashi gives two layers in [Rashi on Genesis 1:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.1.1).

**1. The grammar.** He argues that the word *reshit* in Scripture always appears in the construct state, linked to the word after it. His examples are "the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim," "the beginning of his kingdom," and "the first of your grain." So *bereshit bara Elohim* should be read like *bereshit bro Elohim*, "at the beginning of God's creating." He compares Hosea 1:2, *tchilat diber Hashem be-Hoshea*, "the beginning of the Lord's speaking through Hosea." On this reading the verse is a time-clause: "At the beginning of God's creating heaven and earth, when the earth was formless and void and darkness covered the deep, God said, 'Let there be light.'"

**2. What the verse does not teach.** Rashi says the text "does not intend to teach the order of creation." If it did, it would have said *barishonah*, "at first." He also gives evidence that the order isn't strict. The waters already existed in verse 2, and the heavens were made from fire and water. In his words, the verse "taught nothing about the order of what came earlier and later."

**3. Why "Elohim" and not the Name YHWH.** Rashi says God first intended to create the world through the attribute of strict justice (*midat ha-din*). He saw that the world could not endure that way, so He put the attribute of mercy first and joined it to justice. He cites Genesis 2:4, "on the day that the Lord God [*Hashem Elohim*] made earth and heaven."

## The midrashic layer
Rashi opens with a drash and not with pshat. He says the verse "calls out for interpretation." Our Rabbis read *reshit* as pointing to two things called *reshit* elsewhere:
- The Torah, "the beginning of His way" (Proverbs 8:22).
- Israel, "the first of His increase" (Jeremiah 2:3).

On this reading, the world was created for the sake of Torah and Israel. This is midrash, not pshat, and Rashi presents it that way.

## Why does the Torah start here?
Rashi opens with a question from Rabbi Yitzchak. The Torah is a book of commandments, so why doesn't it begin with "This month shall be for you…" (Exodus 12:2), the first commandment given to Israel? His answer comes from Psalms 111:6, "He declared to His people the power of His works, to give them the inheritance of the nations." If the nations call Israel robbers for taking the land of the seven Canaanite nations, Israel can answer that the whole earth belongs to God. He created it, gave it to whom He pleased, and then took it from them and gave it to Israel.

[Ramban on Genesis 1:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Ramban_on_Genesis.1.1) quotes this and then raises an objection. Beginning with creation is essential and not just a way to defend Israel's claim to the land. It is "the root of faith," and someone who believes the world is eternal "denies the fundamental principle." Ramban's answer is that *Ma'aseh Bereshit* is "a deep secret" that can't be fully understood from the verses alone. It is known through a tradition going back to Moses, and those who know it are obligated to conceal it. So Rabbi Yitzchak's point is that the Torah didn't need to include these details for the sake of faith. Ramban reads the narrative from creation through Eden, the Flood, and the dispersion as showing that God gives and takes away lands according to people's conduct. (I read only the first part of Ramban's long comment, because the retrieved text was cut off.)

## Practical and conceptual bottom line
- **Basic reading:** the world did not create itself and is not eternal. God brought it into being.
- **Rashi's grammatical point** keeps us from building a rigid timeline out of the verse. The verse introduces creation and does not itemize its order.
- **Ramban's emphasis:** creation is the foundation of faith, but its inner workings are not fully open to plain reading.

If you'd like to go further, I can look at Ibn Ezra, at Bereshit Rabbah on the verse, or at the "creation from nothing" question (the word *bara*) once Sefaria is responding again.

Rate limited; retry the failed ones.**Short answer:** Not necessarily. On Rashi's plain-sense reading, the verse doesn't say that heaven and earth came first. It describes what was already there when God began to create, and the waters are already present in verse 2. So the Torah doesn't give a strict order of creation here, and Rashi infers that the water preceded the earth.

(Sefaria was rate-limiting me, so I could only retrieve Rashi and the opening of Ramban on Genesis 1:1. I couldn't pull the verse text itself or the other sources. I mark below what I'm citing from memory.)

## Key Takeaways
- Rashi says Genesis 1:1 doesn't teach the order of creation, so it doesn't say heaven and earth came before everything else.
- He reads *bereishit bara* as "at the beginning of God's creating," with *bereishit* in the construct (possessive) state.
- He argues that the waters, mentioned in verse 2, were created before the earth.
- Rashi also notes that the heavens were made from fire and water. Water is therefore part of the substance of heaven.
- Ramban, in contrast, stresses that Genesis 1 is a deep mystery and cannot be fully learned from the verses alone.

## The verses
[Genesis 1:1–2] reads (quoted from memory, not retrieved): "בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ. וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי תְהוֹם וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם."
"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. The earth was unformed and void, darkness was on the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters."

The question arises because verse 2 mentions "the deep" and "the waters" without ever saying when they were created.

## Rashi's argument
In [Rashi on Genesis 1:1], he first gives the midrashic reading, that the world was created for the sake of the Torah and Israel, both called *reishit* (beginning). Then he turns to pshat (the plain meaning):

- He explains that the verse does not intend "to point out the order of the acts of Creation." If it did, it would have said *bareishonah bara*, "At first God created…".
- His grammatical reason is that *reishit* in Scripture is always in the construct state. Examples are *bereishit mamlekhet Yehoyakim*, "in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim," and *reishit diganekha*, "the first of your grain." So *bereishit bara Elokim* means "at the beginning of God's creating."
- In his reading, the sequence is: at the beginning of creating heaven and earth, the earth was unformed, and there was darkness. Then God said "Let there be light."
- He then answers the objection that the verse really does mean "at the beginning of everything, He created heaven and earth," with a word left out, as in other elliptical verses. Even so, he says: "תְּמַהּ עַל עַצְמְךָ", "be astonished at yourself." The reason is that the waters came first: "שֶׁקָּדְמוּ הַמַּיִם לָאָרֶץ", "the waters preceded the earth."
- His proof is that verse 2 says "the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters," and Scripture never says when the water was created.
- He adds that "the heavens were created from fire and water" (*mei-esh u-mayim*), so water is part of heaven's own substance.
- His conclusion is that Scripture teaches nothing about the order of earlier and later things.

So in Rashi's view, the water was not created after heaven and earth. It was there when the earth was still unformed, and at the very least it preceded the earth. The Torah simply doesn't tell us the chronology.

## Ramban's caution
In [Ramban on Genesis 1:1], Ramban explains why the Torah begins with creation at all. He says creation is "סוֹד עָמֹק", "a deep mystery," not fully understood from the verses. It is known only through the tradition going back to Moses.

Ramban's discussion there is about why the Torah opens with creation. The retrieved text didn't reach his comments on verse 2. I therefore can't tell you what he says there about the waters. He does ask us to be modest about reading a precise chronology off the text.

## Other approaches (from memory, not verified here)
I couldn't retrieve these, so check them yourself:

- **Ibn Ezra** on Genesis 1:1–2 deals with the same question. I recall him treating the waters in verse 2 as already existing, but I haven't verified his wording.
- **The Talmud and midrash** list what was created first. [Chagigah 12a] has a tradition of "ten things created on the first day." I'm not certain of the exact list, so please read it directly.
- **A different reading** takes verse 1 as a summary headline. Verses 2 onward then describe how it happened, with the water already present. This is consistent with Rashi's idea that the verse isn't giving a sequence.

I can retry these sources and go through them with you if you'd like.

answer:
The Torah is traditionally counted as having **304,805 letters** and about **79,976 words**. The Chumash is usually counted at 5,845 verses. I couldn't retrieve a source for these figures from Sefaria just now, so they come from my memory of the standard Masoretic counts. Please treat them as unverified. I did read the Talmudic source for the practice of counting.

## Key Takeaways
- The usual figures are 304,805 letters, about 79,976 words and 5,845 verses.
- The Talmud says the early scholars were called *Soferim* ("counters") because they counted every letter of the Torah.
- The Talmud itself names the middle letter, middle word and middle verse of the Torah.
- Different traditions don't match exactly, because the count depends on spelling (*ḥaser* and *yeter*, "missing" and "extra" letters).

## The Talmudic source
The Gemara in [Kiddushin 30a] says:

> "לְפִיכָךְ נִקְרְאוּ רִאשׁוֹנִים ״סוֹפְרִים״, שֶׁהָיוּ סוֹפְרִים כׇּל הָאוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה"

"Therefore the early [scholars] were called *Soferim*, because they would count all the letters in the Torah."

It then gives the midpoints:
- The *vav* of *gachon* (גָּחוֹן, [Leviticus 11:42]) is the midpoint of the letters of a Torah scroll.
- *Darosh darash* (דָּרֹשׁ דָּרַשׁ, [Leviticus 10:16]) is the midpoint of the words.
- *Vehitgalach* (וְהִתְגַּלָּח, [Leviticus 13:33]) is the midpoint of the verses.

I added the verse locations for these three phrases from memory. They aren't in the passage I retrieved.

## The caveat about exact numbers
In the same passage, Rav Yosef asks whether the *vav* of *gachon* belongs to the first half or the second half. The Gemara answers that the scholars of that era "were experts in *ḥaseirot* and *yeterot*" (words written fully or defectively). It says "we are not experts" in this. So even in the Talmud's day, the exact count depended on the spelling tradition, and our scrolls may not match theirs.

That is why you will see small differences between sources. The totals for words and verses vary slightly, depending on how one counts. For example, some count letters or words differently where the written text (*ketiv*) and the traditional reading (*keri*) diverge. Letter counts are also affected by spelling variants.

The 304,805 figure is the one found in most popular and Masoretic sources. For a precise count, consult a Masoretic work or a *sofer*'s reference. If you tell me which tradition you're asking about, I can look for it.

Rate limited; let me retry a smaller set.Several passages in Tanakh speak of an eternal covenant (*brit olam*) between God and Israel. The Talmud doesn't have one central text on it, but it discusses the idea in several places. Sefaria was rate-limiting me, so I couldn't retrieve the texts and I'm working from memory. The references below are standard, but please check the wording on Sefaria, and I've paraphrased more than I've quoted.

## Key Takeaways
- The phrase *brit olam* (eternal covenant) is attached to three covenants in the Torah: Abraham's (circumcision), Sinai's Shabbat, and the Land.
- Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 4 say God will not break the covenant even after Israel sins and is exiled.
- Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Ezekiel compare God's promise to the fixed order of sun, moon, and mountains.
- The Talmud develops this in the teaching that a Jew remains a Jew even after sinning, and in the debate about when Israel accepted the Torah.

## Tanakh

**The covenant with Abraham.** [Genesis 17:7] says: "וַהֲקִמֹתִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ וּבֵין זַרְעֲךָ אַחֲרֶיךָ לְדֹרֹתָם לִבְרִית עוֹלָם". Translation: "I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, throughout the generations, as an everlasting covenant." The next verse ties the land to this covenant. [Psalms 105:8-10] recalls it, and verse 10 calls it a *brit olam* for Jacob and Israel.

**Shabbat as a sign.** [Exodus 31:16-17] says Israel is to keep Shabbat throughout their generations as a *brit olam*, and that it is "a sign forever" between God and Israel. This is the verse behind the *V'shamru* passage we say on Shabbat.

**The covenant survives sin and exile.**
- [Leviticus 26:44-45] comes at the end of the harsh rebuke. It says that even when Israel is in the land of its enemies, God will not reject them "to destroy them, to break My covenant with them."
- [Deuteronomy 4:31] says God "will not abandon you, nor destroy you, nor forget the covenant of your fathers."
- [Judges 2:1] has God say, "I will never break My covenant with you."

**The prophets.**
- [Jeremiah 31:30-36] compares the covenant to the fixed laws of sun, moon, and sea. The seed of Israel will cease to be a nation before God only if those laws cease. This is probably the most direct statement of permanence. The passage also speaks of a "new covenant" (31:30-33), which the text itself describes as God's Torah written on the heart. It renews the covenant and does not replace it.
- [Isaiah 54:9-10] says the mountains may move, but God's *chesed* (lovingkindness) will not leave Israel, and His "covenant of peace" will not be shaken. See also [Isaiah 59:21] and [Isaiah 55:3].
- [Ezekiel 37:26-27] speaks of a "covenant of peace, an eternal covenant," in the context of the ingathering and rebuilt sanctuary.

**Related eternal covenants.**
- [Leviticus 24:8] says the showbread is a *brit olam*.
- [Numbers 25:13] gives Pinchas a covenant of priesthood forever.
- [Genesis 9:16] is God's eternal covenant with Noah, which covers all living creatures and not only Israel.

## Talmud
- **Israel remains Israel.** [Sanhedrin 44a] teaches *"Yisrael af al pi shechata Yisrael hu"* (Israel, even though it has sinned, is still Israel). This is the classic rabbinic expression of an unbroken covenant.
- **Still God's children.** In [Kiddushin 36a], Rabbi Meir holds that Israel are called "children" of God whether or not they act as such, based on [Deuteronomy 14:1].
- **Voluntary acceptance.** [Shabbat 88a] has the midrash that God held Sinai over Israel "like a barrel," which implies the acceptance was coerced. Rava answers that Israel freely re-accepted the Torah in the days of Ahasuerus (the Purim story). This is a rabbinic way of saying the covenant was renewed willingly.

## Practical note
The eternal covenant is a major theme in the liturgy, including *V'shamru*, the blessing after *Birkat HaMazon*, and the Avot blessing of the Amidah, which mentions remembering the covenant of the fathers. If you tell me which angle interests you, I can retrieve the texts and commentators (Rashi, Ramban, Rambam) once Sefaria is responding again.

answer:
Ich versuche es noch einmal, nacheinander.Das Verbot kommt aus der Tora: Man soll den Bart nicht „verderben“ (*haschchatah*). Nach der Halacha gilt es vor allem für das Rasieren mit einem Rasiermesser oder mit Mitteln, die wie eines wirken. Ein Bart muss nicht lang wachsen. Ob und wie man den Bart trotzdem kürzen darf, hängt von der Methode und von der Gemeinde ab.

**Hinweis zur Quellenlage:** Die Sefaria-Abfragen sind gerade durchgehend fehlgeschlagen (Fehler 429, zu viele Anfragen). Ich konnte die Texte deshalb nicht öffnen und zitiere aus dem Gedächtnis. Die Stellenangaben habe ich nicht überprüft, und Details wie die Einzelmeinungen bei den elektrischen Rasierern solltest du nachprüfen.

## Key Takeaways
- Die Quelle ist ein ausdrückliches Tora-Verbot in [Leviticus 19:27].
- Verboten ist das „Verderben“ der Bartecken, nach der Halacha vor allem mit Rasiermesser oder rasiermesserähnlicher Wirkung.
- Die Tora nennt keinen Grund. Die Kommentatoren verweisen auf die Abgrenzung von götzendienerischen Bräuchen. Die Kabbala sieht im Bart zusätzlich eine geistige Bedeutung.
- Scheren und Elektrorasierer sind unter den Poskim umstritten. Chabad und viele Sefarden sind strenger.
- Für die Praxis brauchst du einen Rabbiner, denn die Methode und der Rasierertyp entscheiden.

## Die Quelle in der Tora
In [Leviticus 19:27] steht: „לֹא תַקִּפוּ פְּאַת רֹאשְׁכֶם וְלֹא תַשְׁחִית אֵת פְּאַת זְקָנֶךָ“. Das heißt: „Ihr sollt den Rand eures Haupthaars nicht rundum scheren, und du sollst den Rand deines Bartes nicht verderben.“

## Was genau ist verboten?
Der Talmud behandelt das in [Makkot 20b–21a]. Nach dem dort Gelehrten gibt es fünf Stellen am Gesicht, an denen das Verbot gilt. Das sind die Bartecken an den Schläfen und am Kiefer sowie die Stelle am Kinn.

Verboten ist das *haschchatah*, also das „Verderben“ des Bartes, und nach der Überlieferung vor allem mit einem Rasiermesser (*ta'ar*). Wer mit einem Rasiermesser rasiert, übertritt das Verbot. Wer nur mit einer Schere kürzt, tut es nach dem Grundsatz nicht, solange die Schere nicht wie ein Rasiermesser wirkt.

Die Codices behandeln das in [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 181] und bei Maimonides im [Mishneh Torah, Idolatry 12]. Dort steht auch, dass ein Schnitt mit zwei Klingen direkt an der Haut (Schere nach Art eines Rasiermessers) dem Rasiermesser gleichgestellt wird.

## Warum? Die Gründe
Die Tora nennt keinen Grund. Es gilt als *chok*, ein Gebot ohne genannten Grund. Die Kommentatoren schlagen aber Erklärungen vor:
- **Abgrenzung vom Götzendienst:** Maimonides erklärt im [Mishneh Torah, Idolatry 12], dass götzendienerische Priester ihren Bart rasierten. Die Tora wollte Israel davon abgrenzen.
- **Würde und Eigenart:** Der Bart gilt in der Tradition als Zeichen von Würde und als Teil des Menschenbildes.
- **Kabbala:** Der Sohar spricht von den „13 Teilen des Bartes“ (*tikkunei dikna*), die für göttliche Eigenschaften stehen. Deshalb lassen manche den Bart auch nicht kürzen, selbst wenn es erlaubt wäre.

## Praxis nach Gemeinden
- **Aschkenasisch:** Rasiermesser sind verboten. Eine Schere ist erlaubt, solange sie nicht rasiermesserartig an der Haut schneidet. Beim Elektrorasierer ist das Bild gemischt. Manche Poskim erlauben bestimmte Geräte mit Schutzgitter, weil die Klinge die Haut nicht berührt. Andere verbieten sie, weil sie wie eine Schere wirken. Rav Mosche Feinstein wird oft als erlaubend genannt, das Chason Isch als strenger. Das habe ich hier nicht überprüft.
- **Sefardisch:** Die Tendenz ist strenger. Viele folgen auch der Kabbala und schneiden gar nicht oder nur sehr zurückhaltend.
- **Chabad:** Hier ist man streng. Man schneidet den Bart gar nicht, auch nicht mit der Schere.

## Das ist keine Pflicht, einen langen Bart zu tragen
Das Verbot betrifft das Verderben der Bartecken. Wer den Bart wachsen lässt oder ihn nur vorsichtig und nach Anweisung seines Rabbiners kürzt, verhält sich anders als jemand, der ihn rasiert. Wer seinen Bart pflegen will, sollte vorher klären, ob sein Gerät und seine Methode erlaubt sind.

Weil es um deine konkrete Methode geht (Rasierer, Schere, Trimmer, Enthaarungscreme), frag bitte deinen Rabbiner. Er kann dir sagen, was für dich und deine Gemeinde gilt.

scores.rationale: La respuesta presenta bien la prohibición tradicional y el responsum del CJLS de 1950 como permiso limitado a ir a la sinagoga. answer:
**Respuesta breve:** No hay una respuesta única, porque el movimiento masorti (conservador) no tiene un criterio uniforme. La postura histórica del Comité de Ley y Normas Judías (CJLS) de Estados Unidos, de 1950, permite conducir hasta la sinagoga en shabat, pero no viajar por ocio o por compras. Muchos rabinos y comunidades masortíes, sobre todo en Israel, son más estrictos. La halajá ortodoxa tradicional prohíbe conducir en shabat sin excepciones.

No pude recuperar de Sefaria todos los textos que quería consultar. Una de las consultas funcionó y las demás fallaron por límite de peticiones. Lo que sigue sobre las responsas masortíes lo resumo de memoria, sin citar textos verificados. Compruébelo en las fuentes originales antes de apoyarse en ello.

## Puntos clave
- **Postura de 1950 (CJLS):** se permite conducir a la sinagoga cuando no hay alternativa razonable, porque se considera que la asistencia al servicio comunitario es esencial para la vida judía.
- **Esa permisión es limitada:** no cubre viajes de recreo, compras ni otras actividades.
- **No es una postura uniforme:** dentro del movimiento hay rabinos que permiten más y otros que prohíben conducir, también hacia la sinagoga. La rama israelí tiende a ser más restrictiva.
- **Ortodoxia:** prohíbe conducir en shabat y no admite la excepción de ir a la sinagoga.
- **Para su caso:** consulte a un rabino de su comunidad.

## La base bíblica
La Torá dice sobre el shabat: «שְׁבוּ אִישׁ תַּחְתָּיו אַל־יֵצֵא אִישׁ מִמְּקֹמוֹ בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי» («Permanezca cada uno en su lugar; que nadie salga de su sitio el séptimo día») [Exodus 16:29]. De ahí la tradición rabínica deriva los límites de desplazamiento (*tejum shabat*, el «límite del shabat»). La Guemará, Maimónides y el Shulján Aruj tratan esas reglas. Mi traducción de la cita es literal y se apoya en la que ofrece Sefaria.

## La postura ortodoxa tradicional
- Conducir es un acto prohibido por varios motivos. Entre ellos están el encendido del motor, que se ve como una forma de «encender» o de «construir», y el desplazamiento fuera del *tejum*.
- Los poskim ortodoxos, tanto asquenazíes como sefardíes, coinciden en esto. Por eso quien guarda shabat según la halajá tradicional vive cerca de la sinagoga y va a pie.
- Esto no cambia por la importancia de rezar con minián.

## La postura masortí (según mi conocimiento)
- **Responsa de 1950.** El CJLS aprobó una responsa que permite conducir a la sinagoga. Sus argumentos principales, según recuerdo:
  - La asistencia a la sinagoga es un valor central. Si las personas vivieran lejos y no pudieran ir, se debilitaría la vida comunitaria.
  - Parte del análisis sostiene que el motor de combustión interna no encaja claramente en las prohibiciones de la Torá, y que la restricción sobre viajar sería de rango rabínico, lo que da más margen a la flexibilidad.
- **Alcance limitado.** Esa responsa no autoriza el uso del auto para actividades de ocio. El ideal declarado es vivir a distancia de la sinagoga que se pueda recorrer a pie.
- **Posturas posteriores.** Después de 1950 hubo otras opiniones dentro del CJLS. Algunas defienden una postura más estricta y otras una más amplia. No recuerdo con precisión los autores ni los años, así que no los cito.
- **Israel.** El movimiento masortí israelí suele pedir más observancia. En general se desaconseja conducir, y la permisión para ir a la sinagoga se considera una excepción para quien no tiene otra opción.

## Resumen por comunidades
| Comunidad | Conducir en shabat |
|---|---|
| Ortodoxa (asquenazí, sefardí, jabad) | Prohibido |
| Masortí/conservador (EE. UU., postura de 1950) | Permitido para ir a la sinagoga cuando no hay alternativa |
| Masortí en Israel | Más restrictivo, con la permisión como excepción |

Esto es una explicación de fuentes y posturas, no una decisión halájica para su caso. Consulte a su rabino, de la comunidad a la que pertenezca, para saber cómo aplicarlo en su situación.

answer:
Rate limit; vou tentar novamente com menos chamadas.Um gentio não tem obrigação de cumprir a mitzvá de sucá. Se quiser sentar-se numa sucá por vontade própria, a Torá não o proíbe e ele recebe recompensa por isso, embora não seja uma mitzvá que o vincule. Essa é a síntese a partir das fontes que consegui consultar. Não consegui abrir o texto de Sucá 28b (limite de acesso da Sefaria), por isso não me apoio nele.

## Pontos principais

- A mitzvá de sucá é dirigida a Israel: "todo cidadão em Israel" habitará em cabanas.
- O gentio está obrigado às sete leis de Noé, não às mitzvot da Torá em geral.
- O Rambam permite que um gentio que queira cumprir uma mitzvá da Torá para receber recompensa o faça, desde que a cumpra como manda a halachá.
- A recompensa é menor que a de quem foi ordenado, segundo Avodá Zará 3a.
- O Rambam proíbe o gentio de criar uma religião ou um "dia de descanso" próprios, mas isso é outra questão (veja abaixo).

## A fonte e o pshat (sentido simples)

O versículo diz: "בַּסֻּכֹּת תֵּשְׁבוּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים, כָּל־הָאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשְׁבוּ בַּסֻּכֹּת" ("Em cabanas habitareis sete dias; todo cidadão em Israel habitará em cabanas") [Leviticus 23:42]. A obrigação recai sobre o povo de Israel. O gentio, por sua vez, está ligado às sete leis de Noé (veja [Sanhedrin 56a]).

## Pode fazê-lo voluntariamente?

O Rambam escreve:

> "בֶּן נֹחַ שֶׁרָצָה לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה מִשְּׁאָר מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה כְּדֵי לְקַבֵּל שָׂכָר. אֵין מוֹנְעִין אוֹתוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ כְּהִלְכָתָהּ."

Tradução: "Um filho de Noé que queira cumprir uma das demais mitzvot da Torá para receber recompensa, não o impedimos de cumpri-la segundo a halachá." [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:10]

O Rambam dá como exemplos o gentio que traz uma oferta de elevação (*olá*) ou que dá *tzedacá*, e ambos são aceitos. Pela lógica dele, sentar-se numa sucá válida com a intenção de cumprir a mitzvá se enquadra nesse princípio. Esta aplicação à sucá é um raciocínio meu a partir do Rambam, não uma citação dele.

## Qual é o "valor" desse cumprimento?

O Talmud discute se os gentios recebem recompensa por mitzvot que não lhes foram ordenadas. Rabi Meir ensina que um gentio que se dedica à Torá é "como um Sumo Sacerdote". A conclusão é que ele recebe recompensa, mas menor:

> "אֵין מְקַבְּלִין עֲלֵיהֶם שָׂכָר כִּמְצֻוֶּה וְעוֹשֶׂה, אֶלָּא כְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצֻוֶּה וְעוֹשֶׂה, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: גָּדוֹל הַמְצֻוֶּה וְעוֹשֶׂה יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁאֵינוֹ מְצֻוֶּה וְעוֹשֶׂה."

Tradução: eles não recebem recompensa como quem é ordenado e cumpre, mas como quem não é ordenado e cumpre. Rabi Chanina diz que quem é ordenado e cumpre é maior do que quem cumpre sem ter sido ordenado. [Avodah Zarah 3a]

Ou seja, o gentio não cumpre a obrigação de sucá no sentido pleno, porque não está obrigado. Mas o ato não é inútil.

## Um detalhe: a sucá e os povos, na Guemará

No mesmo trecho, o Talmud conta que, no futuro, os povos pedirão a Torá. D'us lhes dirá: "מִצְוָה קַלָּה יֵשׁ לִי וְסוּכָּה שְׁמָהּ, לְכוּ וַעֲשׂוּ אוֹתָהּ" ("Tenho uma mitzvá leve, cujo nome é sucá; vão e cumpram-na"). Cada um fará uma sucá no telhado. Então D'us fará o sol queimar, como no solstício de verão (*tekufat Tamuz*), e cada um sairá dando um pontapé na sua sucá. [Avodah Zarah 3a]

Isso é uma passagem aggádica sobre a era futura. Não é uma regra prática. Ela mostra que a sucá é uma mitzvá "leve" por não custar dinheiro, mas que exige entrega, e que por isso é um teste de aceitar o jugo divino.

## Distinção importante: criar uma "religião" própria

O Rambam também escreve que um gentio que se dedica ao estudo da Torá, ou que guarda um dia de descanso como Shabat ou cria uma festa para si, é passível de punição. A regra geral é que "não se permite que eles inovem uma religião nem criem mitzvot para si por conta própria": ou se tornam conversos, ou permanecem na sua lei sem acrescentar nem diminuir [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9]. Esse princípio não é uma proibição de cumprir mitzvot. Os dois halachot se harmonizam pela expressão "כהלכתה" ("conforme a halachá"): o gentio que cumpre uma mitzvá de forma pontual e correta, com sinceridade, é aceito. Já quem institui um sistema religioso novo, ou um "feriado" próprio, extrapola. Os comentaristas debatem o limite exato, e eu não consegui consultá-los aqui.

## Na prática

- Um não judeu que queira entrar na sucá de um amigo judeu como convidado, ou conhecer a mitzvá, não tem nenhum problema.
- Para quem quer cumprir a mitzvá com fidelidade, a sucá deve ser válida (cobertura de *schach*, paredes etc.).
- Um gentio não costuma recitar a bênção "אשר קדשנו במצותיו וציוונו" ("que nos santificou com Suas mitzvot e nos ordenou"), porque ela afirma uma ordem que ele não recebeu. Isso é o que eu entendo da prática, e não consegui verificar a fonte.
- Se a pessoa deseja fazer da Torá o seu caminho completo, o caminho é a conversão através de um beit din reconhecido, e não a prática avulsa de mitzvot.

Para um caso concreto, como um amigo gentio que quer fazer a sucá ou comer nela, ou alguém que pensa em conversão, vale consultar um rabino da sua comunidade.

pitfalls_hit: Oublier la bénédiction finale (Boré nefachot)
scores.rationale: La réponse donne correctement Ha'adama pour la tomate crue ou cuite, avec la bonne distinction halakhique entre arbre et plante annuelle, et cite bien OC 203:1 et 205:1. En revanche, elle omet totalement la bénédiction finale Boré nefachot. Elle reste floue sur Chéhakol pour les produits transformés comme le ketchup et la sauce lisse. Elle ne traite pas non plus la salade de légumes, qu'une seule bénédiction Ha'adama couvre.

answer:
**Réponse directe :** sur une tomate, on dit *Boré péri ha'adama* (בורא פרי האדמה), qu'elle soit crue, en salade ou cuite en morceaux. La tomate pousse sur une plante annuelle, qui ne reste pas d'une année à l'autre. Elle est donc traitée comme un légume, même si botaniquement c'est un fruit.

## Points essentiels
- Tomate crue : *Ha'adama*.
- Tomate cuite : *Ha'adama* aussi, car elle est bonne crue comme cuite.
- Pas de *Ha'etz*, parce que la tomate ne pousse pas sur un arbre.
- Les produits transformés (jus, coulis, ketchup) sont discutés. Il vaut mieux demander à son rav.
- Si la tomate fait partie d'un repas avec du pain, la bénédiction *Hamotsi* la couvre en général.

## Sources et explications

**La règle de base.** Le Choulhan Aroukh écrit : « Sur les légumes, on dit *Boré péri ha'adama*, même s'ils sont crus. De même, pour tous les fruits et légumineuses qui sont bons crus et cuits, on dit après la cuisson la bénédiction qui leur convenait avant. » [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 205:1]
- Le texte cite des exceptions : le chou, la betterave et la courge, qui sont meilleurs cuits que crus. Ils prennent *Shéhakol* crus et *Ha'adama* cuits.
- Il cite aussi l'ail et le poireau, qui prennent *Shéhakol* une fois cuits.
- La tomate n'est dans aucune de ces exceptions, puisqu'on la mange volontiers crue comme cuite. Cette application à la tomate est mon raisonnement, pas une citation du texte.

**Pourquoi pas *Ha'etz*.** La bénédiction générale sur les produits de la terre est *Ha'adama* : « Sur les fruits de la terre, on dit *Boré péri ha'adama* ». [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 203:1] *Ha'etz* est réservée aux fruits d'un arbre, dont le tronc subsiste d'une année sur l'autre. La tomate vient d'un plant qui meurt et qu'on replante, donc c'est *Ha'adama*.

**Jus, sauce, ketchup.** Je n'ai pas pu relire la source sur les jus (Orach Chayim 202), donc je la donne de mémoire.
- La règle générale veut que le jus de fruits ou de légumes (hors olive et raisin) prenne *Shéhakol*. Certains appliquent cette règle au jus de tomate.
- Pour un coulis ou un ketchup très mixé, les avis varient selon la consistance et selon que des morceaux restent. Ne vous appuyez pas sur ma réponse pour ces cas.

## Pratique
La pratique ci-dessus est la même chez les Ashkenazes et les Séfarades, sans divergence connue sur la tomate crue ou en morceaux. Pour les produits transformés, ou si vous avez un doute précis, consultez votre rabbin.

answer:
Reintento las que fallaron.**Respuesta corta:** No. Encender fuego en Shabat está prohibido por la Torá, y eso incluye encender un fósforo, un encendedor o una hornalla. La única excepción importante es el peligro de vida (*pikuaj nefesh*). Aquí no pude consultar el Rambam ni el Shulján Aruj, porque el servidor de Sefaria dejó de responder. Por eso me apoyo solo en las dos fuentes que sí obtuve.

## Puntos clave
- La prohibición viene de la Torá misma: "No encenderéis fuego en ninguna de vuestras moradas en el día de Shabat".
- La Mishná cuenta "el que enciende" (*hamav'ir*) entre las 39 labores (*melajot*) prohibidas.
- Según la opinión mayoritaria, esto abarca también la electricidad y otras formas modernas de encender. Los detalles los decide un rabino.
- Hay que encender las velas **antes** de que empiece Shabat. Sirven para tener luz y para el *oneg* (el deleite) de Shabat.
- Si hay riesgo para una vida, se permite y hasta se debe encender fuego.

## La fuente
**Torá:** [Exodus 35:3]
> לֹא־תְבַעֲרוּ אֵשׁ בְּכֹל מֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
> "No encenderéis fuego en ninguna de vuestras moradas en el día de Shabat." (traducción mía)

**Mishná:** [Mishnah Shabbat 7:2] enumera las labores principales prohibidas, que son 39. Entre ellas figuran "הַמְכַבֶּה. וְהַמַּבְעִיר", es decir, "el que apaga y el que enciende". Quien enciende un fuego lo hace por una de esas labores. Por eso la prohibición no depende de que se quiera cocinar o dar calor. Basta con crear la llama.

## Qué implica en la práctica
Esto es lo que enseña la tradición en general. No pude verificarlo ahora en el código de leyes:
- **Encender o apagar:** ambos están prohibidos. Se encienden las luces o la cocina antes de Shabat, y se dejan así o se preparan de antemano.
- **Electricidad:** la mayoría de las autoridades ortodoxas prohíben encender luces o aparatos eléctricos. Los fundamentos varían, entre ellos el de "encender". Hay desacuerdos sobre los detalles. En eso no hay diferencia práctica entre asquenazíes y sefardíes: ambos lo tratan como prohibido.
- **Velas de Shabat:** se encienden antes de que empiece Shabat, no durante él. Después ya no se puede encender ni mover la llama.
- **Yom Tov (festividad):** la regla es distinta. Se permite cocinar para comer, y en general transferir fuego de una llama que ya existía. Aun así, no se permite crear fuego nuevo.
- **Peligro de vida:** se profana Shabat para salvar una vida, y eso incluye encender fuego si hace falta. El principio se aprende de [Yoma 85b]. No lo recuperé en esta sesión, así que conviene confirmarlo allí. Si hay una urgencia médica, no esperes: actúa primero y consulta después.

## Si tu pregunta era otra
¿Preguntabas por algo concreto, como calefacción, una vela por duelo (*yahrzeit*) o una situación de frío o enfermedad? Cuéntame y lo reviso con las fuentes cuando Sefaria responda de nuevo. Para tu caso personal, consulta a tu rabino.

answer:
**Réponse directe :** Oui, dans le principe. La halakha ne distingue pas ici entre séfarades et ashkénazes. Tant qu'un couple marié respecte les règles de pureté familiale, l'intimité entre les époux est permise dans son principe. La base en est la formule du Rambam : « kiss any organ he desires » (il peut embrasser n'importe quel organe). La halakha encourage aussi la pudeur, le respect mutuel et la retenue. Certains décisionnaires, surtout dans la tradition kabbalistique, sont plus stricts. Je n'ai pas pu vérifier leurs textes ici.

## Points clés
- Le Talmud établit que « tout ce qu'un homme veut faire avec sa femme, il le fait » [Nedarim 20b].
- Le Rambam, base de la pratique séfarade, permet d'embrasser « chaque organe » à condition de ne pas perdre de semence en vain [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9].
- Le Rema reprend le même principe dans le Shulchan Aroukh [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2].
- Les conditions sont les suivantes : la femme n'est pas *nidda* (en période d'impureté rituelle), les deux époux consentent, il n'y a ni contrainte ni dégoût, et la semence n'est pas perdue en vain.
- Dans les cas concrets, il faut demander à un rav.

## Les sources

**1. Le Talmud.** Dans [Nedarim 20b], le Talmud rejette l'avis de Yohanan ben Dehavai, qui voulait restreindre certaines pratiques. Il conclut : « אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּיוֹחָנָן בֶּן דַּהֲבַאי, אֶלָּא כֹּל מַה שֶּׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — עוֹשֶׂה » (la halakha n'est pas comme Yohanan ben Dehavai ; tout ce qu'un homme veut faire avec sa femme, il le fait). La comparaison est celle de la viande : on peut la manger salée, rôtie, cuite ou bouillie.

**2. Le Rambam.** Voici son texte [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9] :
> « כָּל מַה שֶּׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ עוֹשֶׂה… וּמְנַשֵּׁק בְּכָל אֵיבָר וְאֵיבָר שֶׁיִּרְצֶה… וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יוֹצִיא שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה »

Cela signifie : « Il fait tout ce qu'il veut avec sa femme… il embrasse chaque organe qu'il désire… pourvu qu'il ne perde pas de semence en vain. »

Le Rambam ne nomme pas la pratique dont vous parlez. Ce sont les décisionnaires qui appliquent son principe général, « chaque organe », à ce cas.

Il ajoute aussitôt une limite de *hassidout* (piété) : il ne faut pas « alléger sa tête » dans ce domaine. L'homme doit se sanctifier pendant l'intimité et ne pas s'écarter de la manière habituelle du monde.

**3. Le Shulchan Aroukh et le Rema.** Le texte de [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2] contient la même règle. Elle y apparaît dans la glose du Rema : « ויכול לעשות עם אשתו מה שירצה… ומנשק בכל אבר שירצה… ובלבד שלא יוציא זרע לבטלה ». Il ajoute ensuite : « ואע"פ שמותר בכל אלה כל המקדש עצמו במותר לו קדוש יאמרו לו » (même si tout cela est permis, celui qui se sanctifie dans ce qui lui est permis est appelé saint).

Pour les séfarades, la référence est le Rambam et le Shulchan Aroukh. Le principe de base n'est pas contesté entre les communautés. La différence éventuelle porte sur le degré de retenue recommandé, pas sur l'interdiction de principe.

**4. Une position plus stricte, sans interdiction.** Le même passage du Shulchan Aroukh demande une conduite de sainteté, de pudeur et de modération. Le *Arukh HaShulchan* (ashkénaze) encourage aussi à éviter ce qui risque d'amener à une perte de semence [Arukh HaShulchan, Even HaEzer 25:11]. Dans la littérature kabbalistique, que suivent certains séfarades, on trouve des recommandations de retenue plus fortes. Je n'ai pas retrouvé de texte précis à citer. Si cela vous concerne, demandez à un rav de votre communauté si une coutume particulière s'applique.

## Les conditions pratiques
- **Pureté familiale.** Tout contact intime est interdit pendant la période de *nidda*. Les règles précises doivent être posées à un rav.
- **Consentement.** Le Shulchan Aroukh précise qu'on ne doit pas avoir de relations sans l'accord de l'épouse, ni sous la contrainte, ni dans la haine ou l'ivresse [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2]. Dans [Nedarim 20b], une femme se plaint à Rabbi qu'elle a « dressé la table » et que son mari l'a « retournée ». Rabbi répond que la Torah l'a permis. Rav répond de façon analogue. Ces récits montrent que la question du consentement et de l'harmonie dans le couple s'est posée dès l'époque talmudique.
- **Semence.** L'interdit de perdre de la semence en vain reste la limite principale.

Cette réponse est générale. Pour votre situation concrète, ou pour savoir si votre communauté a une coutume plus stricte, consultez votre rabbin.
