answer:
**Non : la Torah n'interdit pas le mariage entre cousins.** Les unions interdites (*arayot*) sont énumérées en Lévitique 18 (et 20), et les cousins germains n'y figurent pas. La Torah elle-même rapporte plusieurs mariages entre cousins, et la halakha les autorise.

## Points clés
- Lévitique 18:6-18 énumère les parents interdits : mère, belle-mère, sœur, demi-sœur, petite-fille, tante paternelle ou maternelle, épouse de l'oncle, belle-fille, épouse du frère, etc. Les cousins n'en font pas partie.
- Jacob a épousé ses cousines Rachel et Léa, et les filles de Tselofkhad ont épousé leurs cousins.
- Ni les Ashkenazes, ni les Séfarades, ni Habad ne considèrent cette union comme interdite par la halakha.
- Des raisons médicales (génétique) peuvent conduire à demander conseil, mais cela relève de la prudence et non d'un interdit de la Torah.

## La Torah ne cite pas les cousins
Le passage s'ouvre par un principe général : « Que nul d'entre vous ne s'approche de sa proche parente (*sheér besaro*) pour découvrir sa nudité » [Leviticus 18:6]. La liste qui suit est précise. Elle mentionne « la sœur de ton père » et « la sœur de ta mère » [Leviticus 18:12-13], ainsi que « la femme du frère de ton père : c'est ta tante » [Leviticus 18:14]. La fille de l'oncle ou de la tante, c'est-à-dire la cousine, n'apparaît nulle part.

Maïmonide résume les mêmes catégories dans [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 2:1]. Il parle de l'épouse du père, du fils, du frère et de l'oncle paternel, et non des cousins.

## La Torah elle-même rapporte des mariages entre cousins
- **Jacob** a épousé Rachel, « fille de Laban, frère de sa mère » [Genesis 29:10-12], donc sa cousine germaine. Il a aussi épousé Léa, sa sœur.
- **Les filles de Tselofkhad** : « Mahla, Tirtsa, Hogla, Milka et Noa, filles de Tselofkhad, devinrent les épouses des fils de leurs oncles (*livné dodéhén*) » [Numbers 36:10-11]. Cela s'est fait « comme l'Éternel l'avait ordonné à Moïse ». L'union entre cousins était donc ici conforme à un ordre divin, pour que les héritages restent dans la tribu.
- **Isaac et Rebecca** étaient aussi des proches parents. Rebecca était la petite-fille de Nahor, frère d'Abraham (voir Genèse 24). Je n'ai pas pu relire ce verset ici.

## Remarques sur la pratique
- **Avant la révélation du Sinaï**, certaines unions que la Torah interdit ensuite étaient pratiquées. Jacob, par exemple, a épousé deux sœurs. L'argument des cousins ne repose donc pas seulement sur les patriarches. Il repose surtout sur le texte de Lévitique 18 et sur Nombres 36, qui date d'après le don de la Torah.
- **Le Talmud** (Yevamot 62b-63a) loue, de mémoire, celui qui « rapproche ses proches », y compris en épousant la fille de sa sœur. Je n'ai pas pu relire ce passage : la source était tronquée et le service de recherche a été limité. Prenez-le comme une indication à vérifier.
- **Les mœurs actuelles** : le mariage entre cousins germains est licite dans toutes les communautés. Certains foyers l'évitent par habitude familiale ou à cause de maladies génétiques. Le dépistage génétique avant le mariage, par exemple via *Dor Yeshorim*, est répandu dans de nombreuses communautés. C'est une démarche de précaution et non un interdit.

## Pour votre cas
Pour une situation personnelle, par exemple un lien de parenté plus complexe (demi-cousins, parenté par remariage) ou une question médicale, consultez votre rabbin. Je n'ai pas pu relire le Choulhan Aroukh (Even HaEzer, simanim 2 et 15), qu'il pourra vous indiquer.

answer:
Using an app to help you is permissible. Relying on an ingredient scan alone to decide that a processed food is kosher is generally not enough. Most poskim and kashrut agencies rely on reliable rabbinic supervision (a *hechsher*), not on the ingredient list. An app is most useful when it reads a hechsher symbol or looks up a product in a certifying agency's database.

I could only retrieve some of the sources I wanted, because Sefaria rate-limited several lookups. I also did not examine any particular app, so what follows is about this type of app in general.

## Key Takeaways
- An ingredient list shows what a company declares, not whether it is kosher.
- Many kosher concerns never appear on a label: the source of an ingredient, shared equipment, and who cooked or milked the food.
- Halacha does not accept a food's status on the word of someone not known to be reliable in kashrut.
- An app is reliable only to the extent that it points to a trusted hechsher or a trusted agency's database.
- Do not use a phone camera on Shabbat or Yom Tov, and consult your rabbi about which agencies and apps to trust.

## Why ingredients alone don't settle it

**1. Hidden sources.**
- Labels say "natural flavors," "glycerin," "enzymes," "mono- and diglycerides," or "gelatin." These can be animal-derived, and the label won't say whether they are kosher.
- Labels also omit processing aids, and may omit what was run on the same equipment.
- Ingredients are also changed or substituted, so a label can differ from what is actually in the package.

**2. Categories where the law depends on who handled the food.** The Shulchan Arukh makes these matters of supervision, not of the ingredients themselves:
- Non-Jewish milk: "חלב שחלבו עובד כוכבים ואין ישראל רואהו אסור שמא עירב בו חלב טמא" ("Milk that was milked by non-Jews and no Jew saw them do so is forbidden, as perhaps non-kosher milk was mixed in") [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 115:1]. The ingredient "milk" looks the same on any label.
- Food cooked by a non-Jew: foods eaten at a king's table that are not eaten raw are forbidden if a non-Jew cooked them, even in a Jew's pots and house [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 113:1]. This is *bishul akum*. A label won't tell you who cooked the food.
- Wine and grape products, and in some communities other items such as alcoholic beverages. The Shulchan Arukh discusses non-Jewish alcoholic beverages, and the Rema notes the lenient custom in Ashkenazi lands [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 114:1]. This is another area where practice differs by community.

**3. Reliability of the source.** The Shulchan Arukh says: "החשוד לאכול דברים האסורים… אין לסמוך עליו בהם" ("One who is suspected of eating forbidden things… one may not rely on his word") [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 119:1]. The Rema adds that some say even a seller whom we simply don't know to be established in keeping kosher should not be relied on for items where there is a concern of prohibition. This is the halachic basis for relying on a known, trusted *hechsher*. A manufacturer's ingredient panel is a statement from a party with no kashrut accountability. An app that interprets it adds a layer of software, which can misread text or use outdated information.

## When an app can legitimately help
- **Reading a hechsher.** An app that identifies a symbol and tells you which agency it is and whether it's reliable can be a useful tool. The question then becomes whether you trust that agency, and that depends on your community and your rabbi.
- **Querying an agency's own database.** Some certifying agencies publish product lists or apps. The reliability comes from the agency, not from the scan.
- **Flagging problems.** An app can warn you that an ingredient is *potentially* non-kosher, such as carmine or animal-derived additives. This is useful as a warning, but the absence of a warning does not make a product kosher.
- **Foods that don't need certification.** Some foods are kosher by nature, such as plain fresh produce, which still needs checking for insects. For these you don't need an app.

## Practical notes
- **Pesach and special categories.** Pesach (*chametz* and *kitniyot*, which differ by Ashkenazi and Sephardi custom), *cholov Yisrael* (milk supervised by a Jew), and *pas Yisrael* (bread baked by a Jew) are community-dependent and need a specific hechsher. A generic ingredient scan cannot address them.
- **Shabbat and Yom Tov.** Don't use a phone or camera on Shabbat or Yom Tov, even to check a label.
- **Regional variation.** Products and formulations differ between countries, so an app's data may not match the product in your hand.

Different communities also trust different agencies, so ask your rabbi which hechsherim and which apps (if any) you should rely on.

answer:
**Short answer:** Between a husband and wife, the classic halachic sources permit anal intercourse. The condition is that it is consensual and that he does not emit seed outside the vagina. The same sources also treat it as something a pious person should not make a habit of. Anal intercourse between two men is a Torah prohibition.

## Key Takeaways
- Between spouses, the Talmud, Rambam and Shulchan Arukh/Rema all say a man may do "whatever he wishes" with his wife.
- The main limit is *hotza'at zera levatalah* (wasting seed). Anal intercourse is allowed only if he does not ejaculate there. Some lenient views allow occasional exceptions, but not as a habit.
- Mutual consent is required. He may not pressure her, and he should appease her until she is willing.
- Modesty and restraint are encouraged as *chasidut* (extra piety), not required as law.
- Anal intercourse between men is forbidden by [Leviticus 18:22].

## The source in the Talmud
The Talmud in [Nedarim 20b] records that "the Sages said: the halakha is not in accordance with Yochanan ben Dehavai." Ben Dehavai had taught that certain ways of marital relations produce flawed children. The Sages ruled instead: "כֹּל מַה שֶּׁאָדָם רוֹצֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — עוֹשֶׂה" ("whatever a man wishes to do with his wife, he may do"). They compare it to meat from the butcher, which he may eat salted, roasted, cooked or boiled.

The same page tells of a woman who complained to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that her husband "turned the table over." This is understood as a euphemism for atypical relations. Rabbi replied: "My daughter, the Torah permitted you to him, and what can I do for you?"

## The codes
- **Rambam:** [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9] says a man may "engage in vaginal or anal intercourse or engage in physical intimacy without relations, provided he does not release seed in vain." He adds that it is "pious conduct" not to act frivolously about this and to sanctify oneself at the time.
- **Shulchan Arukh and Rema:** [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2] has the Rema's gloss. He may have intercourse "בין כדרכה בין שלא כדרכה" ("in the usual way or the unusual way") "so long as he does not ejaculate outside the vagina."
  - The Rema then cites a lenient view: "some are lenient and say that anal intercourse is permitted even if he ejaculates, if it is occasional and not his habit." He presents this as a minority opinion. Ashkenazim generally follow the Rema, and the strict reading of the main view remains the standard one.
  - He closes with the principle that "anyone who sanctifies himself with what is permitted is called holy." He also says a man should not be with his wife constantly, and should keep intimacy modest and private.
- **Consent:** the same se'if says "he may not have intercourse without her consent, and if she is not interested he should appease her until she is interested." This applies to anything intimate, and all the more to something one spouse may find uncomfortable. The "he may do whatever he wishes" language is about what is permitted. It does not override her say.

## Community differences
- **Ashkenazi:** follow the Rema above. Anal intercourse is permitted without ejaculation, and the lenient view for occasional ejaculation is a minority opinion.
- **Sephardi:** Rambam is the base text, and it contains the same condition about not wasting seed. I couldn't retrieve Sephardi poskim such as Rav Ovadia Yosef or the Ben Ish Chai in this session. How strictly they apply the "wasted seed" condition should be checked with a Sephardi rabbi.
- **Chabad:** I didn't retrieve the Shulchan Aruch HaRav on this point, so I can't say whether it differs.
- **Kabbalistic literature:** my understanding is that the Zohar and later mystical sources are much more restrictive, and that some communities take on those stringencies as *chumra*. I didn't retrieve those sources here, so please treat this as unverified.

## Same-sex intercourse
[Leviticus 18:22] says: "וְאֶת־זָכָר לֹא תִשְׁכַּב מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה תּוֹעֵבָה הִוא" ("Do not lie with a male as one lies with a woman; it is an abhorrence"). The tradition understands this as a prohibition on anal intercourse between men. It does not apply to the marital case above. I couldn't retrieve the Talmudic discussion of this verse ([Sanhedrin 54a]) because of a tool error. This is a sensitive area, and a person in this situation should speak with a rabbi who can listen to their circumstances.

## Practical bottom line
For a married couple, this is a matter of permitted-but-not-encouraged conduct. The conditions are mutual willingness, no emission of seed outside the vagina (on the standard view), and modesty. Details such as the exceptions for emission, medical or comfort concerns, and your community's custom vary. Please consult your rabbi for your personal situation. Many rabbis who deal with marital questions are used to answering them discreetly.

answer:
If you slept in your *tallit katan* (small fringed garment), the common Ashkenazi practice is not to make a separate blessing on it in the morning. Instead, you wear it through the morning and have it in mind when you bless on your *tallit gadol*. Practice among Sephardim and others is less uniform, so ask your rabbi. The Rema's rule that a garment worn at night gets no blessing is the main source I could retrieve. The Mishnah Berurah and the later poskim who apply it were not retrievable, so what I say about them is from memory.

## Key Takeaways
- Night is not the time for *tzitzit*, so the Rema says not to bless on a garment worn at night, because a doubt about a blessing is resolved by not saying it.
- Sleeping in a *tallit katan* is permitted, and the Rema says the custom is lenient about it.
- In the morning you never took the garment off and put it on, so the usual practice is no new blessing on it.
- The common solution is to have the *tallit katan* in mind when you bless on your *tallit gadol*, or on a *tallit katan* you put on fresh in the morning.
- Sephardi and Chabad practice may differ, so check with your own rabbi.

## The sources

**Sleeping in tzitzit is permitted.** The Rema writes that one may sleep in a garment with *tzitzit*: "ויש שכתבו שנהגו שלא לשכב בטלית שיש בו ציצית… אך נוהגין להקל לשכב בהם". In my translation: some wrote that the custom is not to sleep in them, so that the mitzvah is not disgraced, but the custom is to be lenient [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 21:3].

**Night is not the time of the mitzvah.** The verse "ורְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ" ("and you shall see it") limits the obligation to daytime [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 18:1]. The Rambam and the Rosh disagree about what happens to a garment worn at night:
- The Rambam says anything worn at night is exempt.
- The Rosh says it depends on what the garment is designated for.

The Rema then rules: "וספק ברכות להקל ע"כ אין לברך עליו אלא כשלובשו ביום והוא מיוחד ג"כ ליום". In my translation: because a doubt about blessings is resolved leniently, one should bless only when wearing it in the daytime and when it is also designated for daytime [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 18:1].

**Why there is no new blessing in the morning.** As I understand the reasoning (this is my explanation, not a quotation), the blessing is made over the act of putting the garment on. If you wore it through the night and never removed it, you did not put it on in the daytime. Some also treat it as a garment already in use, so a doubt about the blessing arises.

**Taking it off and putting it back on.** The Rema's gloss at [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 8:14] says that a person who removes a garment and intends to put it back on right away need not bless again, and that this applies "when a *tallit katan* remains on him". That passage is about a different case: a *tallit gadol* removed during the day. It does not directly answer your question, but it shows that *tzitzit* worn continuously are not blessed again.

## Practical approaches (as I recall them, not verified in the texts)
- **Ashkenazi:** Do not bless separately on the *tallit katan* you slept in. When you put on your *tallit gadol* and say *le-hit'atef ba-tzitzit* (to wrap oneself in tzitzit), have the *tallit katan* in mind too. Where no *tallit gadol* is worn, as with many unmarried men and some communities, some people put on a different *tallit katan* in the morning with a blessing. The Mishnah Berurah discusses this, but I could not retrieve it to cite precisely.
- **Sephardi and Chabad:** Some authorities suggest taking the garment off and putting it on again after dawn with a blessing, or relying on a different garment. I could not retrieve their rulings, so I won't state them as fact.

Because customs differ, please consult your rabbi for your own practice.

answer:
**Short answer:** I couldn't find one fixed, universal formula in the sources I searched. The common practice is an ownership inscription that acknowledges God as the true owner. It usually says "this book is in the possession (*bireshut*) of so-and-so" instead of "this book belongs to so-and-so." Some people add the verse "To the LORD belongs the earth and all it holds." Please treat the exact wording as a custom of individuals and communities, not a ruling.

## Key Takeaways
- The idea behind the custom is that we hold things as stewards, because everything belongs to God.
- The usual wording is "בִּרְשׁוּת פלוני" ("in the domain of so-and-so"), which expresses stewardship and not absolute ownership. This comes from my own knowledge of how inscriptions are usually worded. I could not retrieve a source for it.
- Some people write [Psalms 24:1] in the front of the book. A verse containing God's Name should be treated respectfully, as *shemot* (sacred writings).
- Halakhically you do still own your property, so the inscription is a matter of piety and identification. It isn't a legal necessity.
- This is a custom with no single binding form. Follow your family's or community's practice, and ask your rabbi if you are unsure.

## The idea behind it
The verse is: "לַיהֹוָה הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ, תֵּבֵל וְיֹשְׁבֵי בָהּ" ("The earth is the LORD's and all that it holds, the world and its inhabitants") [Psalms 24:1].

The Mishnah teaches the same principle in the name of Rabbi Elazar of Bartotha: "תֶּן לוֹ מִשֶּׁלּוֹ, שֶׁאַתָּה וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלּוֹ" ("Give Him of what is His, for you and what is yours are His") [Pirkei Avot 3:7]. He cites David's words, "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וּמִיָּדְךָ נָתַנּוּ לָךְ" ("for everything comes from You, and from Your own hand have we given to You").

A person who writes a name in a book to show stewardship is applying this principle. The book is a trust from God, and it was given to us to learn from and look after.

## What people actually write
These are customs I know of. I couldn't verify a specific source for any of them.
- **"Bireshut" wording.** Writing "ברשות" or "בחזקת" before the name means "in the possession of." It claims custody, not absolute ownership.
- **A verse.** [Psalms 24:1] is a natural choice. [I Chronicles 29:14], "for everything comes from You," is another.
- **A request to return the book.** Many inscriptions ask the finder to return a lost book. This matches the usual purpose of a name in a book, which is to identify the owner.

## Practical notes
- **Halacha.** Ownership is legally real. You can lend, sell, and claim a lost book as yours. The "we own nothing" idea is spiritual and ethical. It doesn't cancel property law.
- **God's Name.** If you write a verse that contains God's Name, treat the page as *shemot*. It should not be thrown away, and the book should be handled respectfully. If that concerns you, use wording without a Divine Name, such as "ברשות" and your name.
- **Language.** Hebrew, English, or both are fine. Use whatever your family or community does.

I wasn't able to search the major halakhic works for a specific ruling on this. If you want a particular text or wording, ask your rabbi or check your family's old *sefarim*. Their inscriptions often show the local custom.

It omits the Pesach–Tisha B'Av weekday connection (476:2) and Taanit 30a. It also only hedges on the roundness and no-mouth reasons. The irrelevant date remark slightly detracts from the structure.

answer:
The egg and the ashes are two separate customs that people often combine. The egg is a mourner's food, so it expresses mourning for the Temple. The ashes recall a verse in Lamentations about suffering and humiliation. Today's date is 23 November 2026, so Tisha B'Av is months away, but the sources are below.

## Key Takeaways
- The egg is a *ma'achal avelim* (mourner's food), so eating it on erev Tisha B'Av is a sign of mourning.
- Dipping in ashes is a separate custom, recorded by the Rema as a stringency of "some," and it is linked to a verse in Lamentations.
- Neither custom is a basic obligation. The Shulchan Arukh's baseline for the final meal is plain bread, salt, and water.
- The idea that the egg's roundness represents the cycle of mourning or of life is a popular explanation. I did not retrieve a source for it in this session.

## The egg: food of mourners
The Shulchan Arukh rules: "נוהגים לאכול עדשים עם ביצים מבושלים בתוכם שהם מאכלי אבלים" ("We customarily eat lentils with cooked eggs in them, which are the food of mourners"). The Rema adds: "ויש נוהגים לאכול ביצים קשים שהוא גם כן מאכל אבלים" ("Some are accustomed to eat hardboiled eggs, which are also a food of mourners") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:5].

So the egg represents mourning because it is what mourners traditionally eat after a death, in the *se'udat havra'ah* (the meal of consolation). The Talmud's source for this is in Bava Batra 16b, which discusses lentils and eggs as mourners' food. I could not retrieve that page here, so I am not quoting it. The popular reasons given for this food are its roundness (the cycle of mourning) and the fact that it has no "mouth" (a mourner is silent). Those explanations appear in later literature, and I haven't verified a specific source for them.

## The ashes: "and He ground my teeth on gravel"
The Rema on the next *se'if* is the source for ashes: "ויש מחמירים לטבל אחר אכילה פת באפר ולאכלו על שם ויגרס בחצץ וגו'" ("There are those who are strict to dip bread in ashes after eating, and to eat it in reference to 'And He has broken my teeth with gravel…'") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:6]. The verse is from Lamentations 3:16, which I couldn't retrieve here. The ashes recall the bitterness and degradation of the destruction, and ashes are also an ancient sign of mourning.

The Rema says to dip **bread** in ashes. The common practice of an egg dipped in ashes is a later combination of the two customs. The egg is the mourner's food, and the ashes are the sign of grief. Communities differ on whether they do this at all.

## Context: this is more than the basic law
- The baseline for the *se'udah hamafseket* (the final meal before the fast) is: "מי שאפשר לו לא יאכל בסעודה המפסקת אלא פת חריבה במלח וקיתון של מים" ("One who is able should eat only dry bread with salt and a flask of water") [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:6].
- Rambam describes the practice of the early pious: dry bread in salt, soaked in water, eaten while "sitting between the oven and the stove… in worry, desolation, and tears, as one whose dead lies before him." He says this is the standard for sages, and that the general public does not take on so much [Mishneh Torah, Fasts 5:9]. The phrase "as one whose dead lies before him" shows the intended spirit: the meal is meant to put us in the state of an *onen* (a mourner before burial).
- Rambam also says that in his time they did not eat even a lentil dish on erev Tisha B'Av unless it fell on Shabbat [Mishneh Torah, Fasts 5:9]. The Shulchan Arukh records the lentil-and-egg custom, which shows that practice varied.

If you want to follow the custom, ask your rabbi how your community does it. Some people eat the egg plain and some dip it in ashes.

The answer directly rejects the premise and correctly explains that Yom Tov Sheni rests on the binding enactment of Beitzah 4b. It gives the mainstream two-day ruling for visitors, with privacy, via Mishnah Berurah 496:13, and covers the Israeli-abroad case and intent to return versus settle. It mentions the Chacham Tzvi only tentatively as a minority view, does not note that Shulchan Arukh HaRav leans toward one day, and omits the hybrid approach. Its Chabad treatment is thin and misses Chabad's distinctive approach, and it does not cite Mishnah Pesachim 4:1.

answer:
Short travel time doesn't change the halacha, because the second day isn't based on distance or on how hard it is to get home. It rests on *minhag avoteinu* (the custom of our ancestors), and the Talmud says it stays binding even though the calendar is now fixed. The mainstream ruling is that a visitor from abroad who plans to go home keeps two days, but does so privately and discreetly in Israel. Your practical concern is real, though, and the halachic literature answers it with some accommodations.

## Key Takeaways
- The second day of Yom Tov today is a rabbinic custom, and the Talmud preserves it as binding custom, not as a response to doubt about the date.
- Because the reason doesn't depend on travel conditions, faster flights don't weaken it.
- Mishnah Berurah rules that a visitor who intends to return keeps two days, but prays and observes Yom Tov privately in his own quarters.
- A person who intends to settle in Israel permanently follows Israeli practice.
- A minority of authorities were more lenient, but this isn't the accepted practice. Anyone with a specific situation should ask a rabbi.

## The source: why the second day exists at all
The Gemara in [Beitzah 4b] asks why we keep two days now that the calendar is fixed. In the old days, the new month was set by witnesses and messengers carried the news, so distant communities weren't sure which day was the 15th. It answers:

"מִשּׁוּם דִּשְׁלַחוּ מִתָּם: הִזָּהֲרוּ בְּמִנְהַג אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם בִּידֵיכֶם, זִמְנִין דְּגָזְרוּ הַמַּלְכוּת גְּזֵרָה וְאָתֵי לְאִקַּלְקוּלֵי"

"Because they sent from there [Eretz Yisrael]: Be careful with the custom of your ancestors in your hands, for sometimes the government may issue a decree and [the calendar] may become confused."

So the second day is a custom of the ancestors that the Sages explicitly wanted kept. Better communication, and now flights, don't remove it. The Gemara already knew that the calendar was fixed ("we know the fixing of the month") and still kept the second day.

## The ruling for visitors
The Shulchan Arukh sets out the mirror-image case, an Israeli who travels abroad. He is forbidden to do *melacha* (prohibited labor) on the second day in an inhabited area "even if he intends to return" [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 496:3]. The same logic is applied in reverse to the visitor from abroad.

The Mishnah Berurah states it directly:

"ובן חו"ל שבא לא"י אם דעתו לחזור למקומו צריך לעשות שני ימים יו"ט ומ"מ תפלת יו"ט צריך להתפלל בביתו בצנעא אכן אם דעתו שלא לחזור למקומו לעולם יתנהג כבני א"י" [Mishnah Berurah 496:13]

"A Diaspora resident who came to Eretz Yisrael, if he intends to return to his place, must keep two days of Yom Tov. Nevertheless, he should pray the Yom Tov prayer in his home, in private. But if he intends never to return to his place, he behaves like the residents of Eretz Yisrael."

The same source gives the principle behind this. Where a practice is private (*davar shebetzin'a*), he need not adopt the local stringency. Where it is public (*pirhesya*), he should avoid making a scene. The Mishnah Berurah applies this to Israelis abroad, for example wearing Yom Tov clothes because that is public. By the same logic, the Diaspora visitor in Israel keeps the day quietly. In practice:
- He doesn't do *melacha* on the second day.
- He doesn't ask Israelis to do *melacha* for him.
- He does not make a public display of it, and he prays in private.

## Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Chabad
- **Ashkenazi:** this follows the Mishnah Berurah above. This is the standard view among Ashkenazi poskim.
- **Sephardi:** this rests on the same Shulchan Arukh and Mishnah Berurah framework, and the mainstream Sephardi practice also keeps two days privately. I did not retrieve Rav Ovadia Yosef's or the Ben Ish Chai's text this time, so I won't quote them.
- **Chabad:** Chabad also keeps two days for a visitor, but I have not checked Shulchan Aruch HaRav on this here.

## Is a more lenient view possible?
There is a minority position. As I recall, the Chacham Tzvi (responsum 167) leaned toward treating the visitor as a local, but I did not retrieve it, so I won't present it as established. It is not the mainstream ruling in practice. A lenient view that is cited by one authority doesn't become the default because of convenience. If someone is relying on a view like that, they should ask their own rabbi.

## What "impractical" does and doesn't change
- **It doesn't change** the underlying obligation, because the rationale in Beitzah 4b is about custom and Sages' decree, not about geography.
- **It does make** the question more common. More people from abroad are in Israel at Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot, so rabbis have developed practical guidance, such as hotels with Yom Tov arrangements, private prayer, and eating in a room or sukkah arranged for the purpose.
- **Intent to return matters most.** Someone who is truly relocating (for example, making *aliyah*) is treated as an Israeli. The Mishnah Berurah adds that if someone moves with his family to earn a living there, we generally assume he has no intention to return. Yeshiva-year students, long-term visitors, and people who are "not sure" are exactly the cases to ask a rabbi about.

As this is practical halacha, please consult your rabbi about your own situation, especially if you are traveling for an extended period or are unsure whether you'll return.

answer:
Rate limited; retry once.Gambling is not a flat prohibition in the codes. Halacha treats it as a serious problem: it is *avak gezel* ("shade of theft"), it is a waste of time, and a professional gambler is disqualified as a witness. The accepted practice, especially for Ashkenazim, is lenient for occasional gambling by someone who has a regular trade. Raffles and lotteries are discussed separately by modern poskim. I couldn't retrieve those responsa because the search tool failed, so what I say about them is general and unverified.

## Key Takeaways
- The Mishnah disqualifies a *mesachek bekuvya* (dice-player) as a witness. [Sanhedrin 24b]
- The Gemara gives two reasons: *asmachta* (the loser never fully commits to pay) and that gamblers do not contribute to "the settling of the world."
- The Rema says the custom is to be lenient. Only someone with no other trade is disqualified. [Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 370:3]
- Charity raffles and commercial lotteries differ from gambling in important ways, but their rulings depend on the setup, and poskim differ.
- Heavy or habitual gambling is discouraged by everyone, and many Orthodox authorities forbid it.

## The Talmudic source
The Mishnah lists those disqualified as witnesses: "הַמְשַׂחֵק בְּקוּבְיָא" ("one who plays with dice"), along with usurers, pigeon-racers and traders in Sabbatical-year produce. [Sanhedrin 24b]

The Gemara asks why the dice-player is disqualified and gives two answers:
- **Rami bar Chama:** It is *asmachta*. Each player stakes money on an uncertain outcome, so neither fully commits to give it, and a transfer made under *asmachta* is not binding. The winner therefore takes money he has not truly acquired.
- **Rav Sheshet:** It is not *asmachta*. The problem is that the gambler is "not engaged in the settling of the world" (*yishuvo shel olam*).

The difference between them is a gambler who has learned another trade. Rabbi Yehudah in the Mishnah disqualifies only someone whose sole occupation is gambling. [Sanhedrin 24b]

## Rambam
The Rambam says a dice-player is disqualified "if he has no trade other than it." He explains that such a person is presumed to live off the winnings, which are *avak gezel*. The rule extends to games with nut shells and pomegranate shells, and to games where animals are raced and the winner takes both stakes. He says the disqualification is rabbinic. [Mishneh Torah, Testimony 10:4]

## Shulchan Arukh and Rema
The Shulchan Arukh brings the view that playing dice with a non-Jew is not theft. It is still forbidden as an idle pursuit (*devarim betelim*), since a person should spend his life on wisdom and the settling of the world. Others hold the player is disqualified only if he has no other trade.

The Rema adds that with another trade, even gambling with a fellow Jew does not disqualify. He then says: "וכבר פשט המנהג כסברא האחרונה לשחוק בקוביא" ("the custom has already spread like the latter view, to play dice"). Only a person whose sole occupation is gambling is disqualified. [Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 370:3]

On the *asmachta* question, the Rema in [Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 207:13] records several approaches:
- The first view is that gambling is not *asmachta*. The outcome is not in either player's hands, so each presumably commits fully, "מספק" (out of doubt).
- That applies when the money is on the table. Gambling on credit (*be'emna*) does not obligate the loser, and a pledge does not help.
- If the money is on the table, another view allows it, while others forbid playing in any case.
- Some say the table must belong to both players.

## Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Chabad
This is my summary, not a retrieved text, so check it with your rabbi.
- **Ashkenazi:** The Rema's custom is the basis for leniency. Many later authorities nevertheless discourage regular gambling as wasted time.
- **Sephardi:** The Shulchan Arukh brings the lenient view as the "other opinion," so Sephardim are generally more careful here. I did not retrieve Rav Ovadia Yosef or the Ben Ish Chai on this, so I won't quote them.
- **Chabad:** I didn't check Shulchan Aruch HaRav on this point.

## Raffles and lotteries
This part is general and not tied to retrieved sources.
- **Charity raffles:** Many contemporary poskim are more lenient. Participants give money knowing it goes to a worthy cause, and the "prize" is secondary. Others are concerned about *asmachta* and about the raffle being a form of gambling.
- **Commercial or state lotteries:** These are generally treated more strictly, but opinions vary.
- **Conditions that matter:** The details can affect the ruling. These include whether the prize is announced and funded in advance, whether the organizer takes a profit, and whether the "ticket" is a real purchase.
- **Shabbat and Yom Tov:** Even where a raffle is permitted, handling money, writing names and buying or selling on those days raise separate issues.

For a specific raffle or lottery, ask your rabbi, since the details of the setup decide the ruling.

answer:
I couldn't find this saying in the Talmud, the Rambam, or the Shulchan Arukh. It appears to be a popular saying about the merit of attending a *pidyon haben* (the redemption of a firstborn son). I couldn't verify who first said it, so I wouldn't present it as established halacha. Attending is still a real mitzvah of joy and honor.

## Key Takeaways
- I found no source for the "80 fasts" saying in the classic texts I could check, and my searches of Sefaria returned nothing for it.
- Treat it as a popular expression of the merit of joining a *seudat mitzvah* (a meal celebrating a mitzvah). It is not a literal halachic equivalence.
- The Rema records a custom to hold a festive meal at the pidyon. This is the real halachic basis for the gathering.
- Don't take the saying as permission to skip real fasts, and don't treat the number as exact.

## What the sources say
**The mitzvah itself.** A father must redeem a firstborn son (one who is the mother's first birth) from a *kohen* (priest) for five *sela'im* (silver coins). The Shulchan Arukh gives the blessings and procedure in [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 305:10].

**The meal.** The Rema's gloss there says: "ויש שכתבו שנהגו לעשות סעודה בשעת הפדיון". In my translation: "Some write that they were accustomed to make a meal at the time of the redemption." He also records that the kohen makes a blessing on wine right after the pidyon, "כדי לפרסומי מלתא", meaning to publicize the matter.

So the classic sources give the pidyon a public, festive setting. They say nothing about a numerical fasting reward.

## Where the "80 fasts" idea likely comes from
This part is my own explanation, not a sourced claim. Sayings like this usually express a few real ideas:
- **Seudat mitzvah.** Joining a meal for a mitzvah is itself a mitzvah, and Jewish tradition attaches great merit to it.
- **Honoring a mitzvah.** Gathering publicly honors the mitzvah, which is also the reason the Rema gives for the wine.
- **Merit-sayings in general.** Popular teachings often use "like fasting X fasts" to convey weight, not to give an exact conversion.

If you've seen it in a particular book, tell me which one and I'll try to look at the wording. Some such sayings are in later kabbalistic or customs literature that I couldn't retrieve here.

## Practical note
If you're invited, go and rejoice with the family. That is a real mitzvah and a real merit. Fasts you are obligated to keep, or have taken on yourself, are not replaced by attending. For questions about your own situation, consult your rabbi.

scores.rationale: The answer separates the biblical Shemini Atzeret from the later Simchat Torah. It explains the Israel/Diaspora difference and Megillah 31a's reading, notes the triennial cycle, and documents medieval customs through the Tur, Shulchan Arukh, Rema and Mishnah Berurah. It does not trace hakafot to 16th-century Safed or Kabbalistic influence; it only says it could not date them. Some phrasing ("the holiday itself is biblical", "the day itself is not new") blurs the fact that the Diaspora Simchat Torah day is rabbinic, and a few quoted wordings (Tur, Rema on minors) are unverified.

answer:
You're right that the name and the celebrations are later, but the day itself is not new. The Torah commands Shemini Atzeret, and the Talmud already has Vezot HaBracha read on the day after it. The name "Simchat Torah," the dancing and the hakafot (circuits with the Torah scrolls) developed in the post-Talmudic and medieval periods.

## Key Takeaways
- The holiday itself is biblical: Shemini Atzeret, the "eighth day" after Sukkot.
- The Talmud already prescribes reading *Vezot HaBracha* on the day after Shemini Atzeret in the Diaspora.
- Its character as a celebration of finishing the Torah is a later custom.
- The Rema (Ashkenazi) records the hakafot, the many aliyot and the children's aliyah.
- In Israel Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah fall on the same day. In the Diaspora they are two days.

## 1. The biblical root: Shemini Atzeret
The Torah has no "Simchat Torah." It has a separate festival right after Sukkot:

> "שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֔ים תַּקְרִ֥יבוּ אִשֶּׁ֖ה לַיהֹוָ֑ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁמִינִ֡י מִקְרָא־קֹ֩דֶשׁ֩ יִהְיֶ֨ה לָכֶ֜ם... עֲצֶ֣רֶת הִ֔וא כׇּל־מְלֶ֥אכֶת עֲבֹדָ֖ה לֹ֥א תַעֲשֽׂוּ"
> "Seven days you shall bring offerings by fire to GOD. On the eighth day you shall observe a sacred occasion... it is a solemn gathering: you shall not work at your occupations." [Leviticus 23:36]

Nothing in the verse mentions the Torah or its completion.

## 2. The Talmudic layer: the reading of *Vezot HaBracha*
The Gemara in [Megillah 31a] lists the readings for each festival:

> "יוֹם טוֹב הָאַחֲרוֹן קוֹרִין 'כׇּל הַבְּכוֹר'... לְמָחָר קוֹרִין 'וְזֹאת הַבְּרָכָה', וּמַפְטִירִין 'וַיַּעֲמֹד שְׁלֹמֹה'"
> "On the last festival day they read 'All the firstborn'... on the next day they read 'And this is the blessing,' and as haftarah 'And Solomon stood.'"

So by Talmudic times, in the Diaspora, the second day (the added day of Yom Tov) was already the day for reading the end of the Torah. The Gemara gives no sign of a celebration, though. The reading was fixed to the festival, and the joy came later.

Based on my own background knowledge, which I could not verify here, this reading fits the Babylonian custom of completing the Torah in one year. The Land of Israel followed a roughly three-year cycle at the time, so the completion fell on a different date.

## 3. Medieval development: the name and the celebration
The Tur ([Tur, Orach Chayim 669]) records the day's order. He says they read *Vezot HaBracha* and then begin Bereishit immediately:

> "וְקוֹרִין אוֹתוֹ שִׂמְחַת תּוֹרָה לְפִי שֶׁמְּסַיְּמִין בּוֹ הַתּוֹרָה וְרָאוּי לִשְׂמוֹחַ בְּסִיּוּמָהּ"
> "They call it Simchat Torah because they finish the Torah on it, and it is fitting to rejoice at its completion."

He gives a reason for starting again at once: "so that Satan will have no opening to accuse, saying: they have already finished it and do not want to read it any more." He adds that Ashkenazi custom has the one who finishes and the one who begins pledge donations and host a festive meal.

I recall that the name appears in the Geonic period, but I couldn't retrieve a source for that.

## 4. The Shulchan Arukh and the Rema
[Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 669:1] sets the law. In the Diaspora, on the ninth day:
- Three scrolls are taken out.
- The first is read from *Vezot HaBracha* to the end of the Torah.
- The second is read from *Bereshit* through "asher bara Elokim la'asot" ([Genesis 2:3]).
- The third is the maftir, the same as the previous day.
- The haftarah is "Vayehi acharei mot Moshe" ([Joshua 1:1]).

The **Rema** (Ashkenazi) adds customs, each one introduced as a custom and not as a law:
- The day is "called Simchat Torah because we rejoice," with a festive meal for the completion of the Torah.
- Many places take out all the Torah scrolls at night and in the morning and sing songs and praises.
- "They circle the bimah with the Torah scrolls just as they circle with the lulav" (the hakafot), all "out of joy."
- Many people are called to the Torah, and the same section is repeated. The Rema says there is no prohibition in this.
- All the children are called up, with the reading "ha-Malakh ha-Go'el" ([Genesis 48:16]).
- Even a minor may finish the Torah, though some say it should be a scholar.

The Rema ends many of these with "every place according to its custom." The [Mishnah Berurah 669:1] adds that the one who reads the last section is called *Chatan Torah* ("groom of the Torah"). It is customary to sell this portion and the *Bereshit* portion, and "it is fitting that the buyers be crowned with Torah, or at least among the leaders of the community."

## 5. Practice today
- **Israel:** Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah are one day. *Vezot HaBracha* is read that day.
- **Diaspora:** Shemini Atzeret is the first day, and Simchat Torah is the second.
- **Hakafot:** Ashkenazi communities generally hold hakafot the night before and on the day of Simchat Torah. Other communities differ in the number of hakafot and in their melodies and piyutim. I have not verified specifics for Sephardi or Chabad practice, so I'm not describing them here. Please ask your community's rabbi.

**Summary of "newness":** the day and its Torah readings are ancient, the name and the central rejoicing are medieval, and many of the dancing customs have been elaborated over the centuries. I could not retrieve sources for the precise dates of the earliest hakafot. A deeper search of Geonic and medieval sources, such as Machzor Vitry, would clarify that.

For practical questions about your own community's customs, consult your rabbi.

answer:
Neither the Talmud nor the Shulchan Arukh, as far as I could verify, says anything about a wife's physical height compared to her husband's. There is no prohibition and no stated preference. The nearest source is a Talmudic principle about marrying "down a step", which later authorities understood in terms of social standing, not stature.

## Key Takeaways
- I found no halachic source that addresses a wife being physically taller than her husband, and I found no prohibition.
- The Talmud says a man should "descend a step" when choosing a wife [Yevamot 63a].
- Rashi explains that this means status, so that she will accept his authority.
- Some people read this as height by analogy. That is a modern association and not what the source says.

## The closest source
After a series of statements by Rabbi Elazar on marriage, [Yevamot 63a] gives proverbial advice on timing and choosing:

- "מתון נסיב איתתא" means "Be patient (deliberate) in taking a wife."
- "נחית דרגא נסיב איתתא. סק דרגא בחר שושבינא" means "Descend a step when taking a wife; ascend a step when choosing a groomsman."

Rashi says "descend a step" means: "לא תקח אשה חשובה ממך שמא לא תתקבל עליה". In my translation: "Do not take a wife who is more important than you, lest she not be accepted by [you / not submit to you]." The phrase is ambiguous, but his point is that the concern is social standing. He does not mention height. [Rashi on Yevamot 63a]

## What this does and doesn't mean
- **Pshat:** The advice is about status, such as lineage, learning and wealth. It is a counsel of prudence for harmony, not a law. The sentence is a proverb and not a halachic ruling.
- **Height by analogy:** People sometimes apply "a step down" to height or age. I did not find a classical source that does so, so treat that as folk usage and not Torah teaching.
- **The real halachic criteria:** The Shulchan Arukh's marriage guidance in Even HaEzer 2 concerns family health and character. For example, [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 2:7] discusses avoiding families with a pattern of certain diseases. Height is not on the list.

## Practical note
Height is not a halachic factor in choosing a spouse. The classical emphasis is on character, compatibility and mutual honor. The Talmud's own reading of "ezer kenegdo" fits that emphasis: "זכה — עוזרתו, לא זכה — כנגדו", meaning if he merits, she is his helper, and if not, she opposes him [Yevamot 63a].

scores.rationale: The core practical guidance is correct and well sourced: put tefillin on now, before sunset, with a beracha, then pray Mincha wearing them, and check local zmanim. It omits several important points. It does not say the morning Shema time has passed, gives no guidance on tashlumin for a missed Shacharit, and offers no bein hashmashot nuance or Rabbeinu Tam tefillin. It also claims there are no community differences while overlooking Rabbeinu Tam practice and the kabbalistic custom regarding tefillin at Mincha.

answer:
**Yes, you can still put on tefillin today, but only until sunset (*shkiah*). Put them on first, then pray Mincha while wearing them.** Check your local sunset time now. Late November in Mexico City it is usually a bit before 6 pm, so you don't have much time.

## Key Takeaways
- Tefillin can be worn all day, and the time ends at sunset.
- Don't wait. If sunset arrives before you put them on, you can't do it tonight.
- Order: put on tefillin, then Mincha with them on, then remove them.
- Mincha is a good reason to put them on now, because a man should have tefillin on during the Amidah.

## Source for the time
The Shulchan Arukh sets the start of the time: "The time to put them on in the morning is when one can see his close friend from four cubits away and recognize him" [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 30:1]. The mitzvah itself lasts through the day: "מצותן להיותם עליו כל היום", "it is a mitzvah to have them on all day" [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 37:2].

The same passage says that, because it is hard to keep a clean body and a focused mind, the custom is not to wear them all day. It adds: "מ"מ צריך כל אדם ליזהר בהם להיותם עליו בשעת ק"ש ותפלה". This means that every person must make sure to have them on during Shema and the Amidah.

The cutoff is stated in [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 30:2]: "אסור להניח תפילין בלילה", "it is forbidden to put on tefillin at night." The reason given is that one might forget he has them on and fall asleep in them. The same se'if allows tefillin put on before sunset to stay on after dark. So the practical deadline is sunset.

I couldn't retrieve exact zmanim for you because I don't have your location confirmed. Please check a local zmanim source for today's sunset in Mexico City.

## Order
1. **Put on tefillin.** Do this with the usual blessings and the usual order: arm tefillin first, then head. This is the standard practice for tefillin put on later in the day. Ask your rabbi if you have a specific custom or doubt about the blessings.
2. **Pray Mincha with the tefillin on.** This follows [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 37:2] above. Ashrei and the Amidah are all done with tefillin on.
3. **Remove them** after Mincha, once you are done.

If you are short on time before sunset, put on the tefillin first and pray after. Don't pray Mincha first, because that would waste the time you have left.

## Community differences
I'm not aware of any Ashkenazi, Sephardi, or Chabad difference on the main points here. All agree on the daytime limit and on having tefillin on during prayer. Some details, such as the blessings or whether to say Shema, may differ by custom.

Please consult your rabbi for your personal situation.

answer:
**Краткий ответ.** В Мишне сказано: «Молящийся и ошибшийся — это для него дурной знак» (*siman ra*). Иерусалимский Талмуд уточняет это слова рава Аха бар Яакова «только в *Авот*», то есть в первом благословении Амиды. Дурным знаком считается ошибка именно там, а не в любом месте молитвы. Обычно это понимают так: дурной знак — это намёк на то, что молитва может быть не принята, а не приговор.

## Главное
- Мишна ([Mishnah Berakhot 5:5]) называет ошибку в молитве «дурным знаком». Для *шалиах цибур* (ведущего молитву) это дурной знак для тех, кто его послал.
- Иерусалимский Талмуд ([Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 5:5]) ограничивает это правило первым благословением, *Авот*.
- Тот же отрывок рассказывает, как р. Ханина бен Доса узнавал по «беглости» своей молитвы, будет ли больной жить. Там же говорится, что важна сосредоточенность.
- Вавилонский Талмуд ([Berakhot 34b]) приводит то же ограничение от имени р. Хии, р. Сафры и «одного из дома рабби», и оно связано с требованием *каваны*, то есть сосредоточенности.
- Практически [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 101:1] требует сосредоточиться хотя бы в *Авот*. Само «дурное знамение» не создаёт отдельного закона.

## Что сказано в Мишне
> «הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל וְטָעָה סִימָן רַע לוֹ. וְאִם שְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר הוּא סִימָן רַע לְשׁוֹלְחָיו, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁשְּׁלוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כְּמוֹתוֹ»

«Молящийся и ошибшийся — для него это дурной знак. А если он посланник общины — это дурной знак для пославших его, ибо посланник человека подобен самому человеку» (мой перевод).

Затем Мишна рассказывает о р. Ханине бен Доса. Он молился о больных и говорил: «этот будет жить, а этот умрёт». Его спросили, откуда он знает. Он ответил: «Если молитва *шгура* (отточена, «течёт») у меня во рту, я знаю, что она принята; если нет — знаю, что она отвергнута (*метурап*)».

## Что добавляет Иерусалимский Талмуд
> «רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב אָמַר וּבִלְבַד בְּאָבוֹת»

«Рав Аха бар Яаков сказал: но только в *Авот*» ([Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 5:5]).

Комментаторы объясняют это так:
- *Пней Моше*: имеется в виду ошибка в благословении *Авот*, потому что оно первое, и в нём необходимо сосредоточиться.
- *Сирилио*: именно ошибка в *Авот*, которое открывает молитву, — это намёк, что человек «не желает их» (то есть не желает отцов, «Авот»). Это трактовка комментатора, а не текст Талмуда.
- Мареh а-Паним сопоставляет это с Вавилонским Талмудом и считает, что спора здесь нет. Мишна тоже говорит об *Авот*, поскольку именно там нужна кавана.

## Параллель в Вавилонском Талмуде
Гемара ([Berakhot 34b]) спрашивает: «Про что (говорит Мишна)?» Рав Хия от имени рава Сафры, который передал слова «одного из дома рабби», отвечает: «в *Авот*». Рядом приводится барайта: молящийся должен сосредоточиться во всех благословениях, а если не может во всех, то хотя бы в одном. И снова «в *Авот*».

## Как понимать «дурной знак»
- Иерусалимский Талмуд сразу переходит к теме сосредоточенности. Р. Шмуэль бар Нахмани говорит: если ты смог направить сердце в молитве, тебе возвещено, что она услышана. Он ссылается на стих «תָּכִין לִבָּם תַּקְשִׁיב אָזְנֶךָ» («Ты укрепишь их сердце, приклонишь Своё ухо», Псалмы 10:17).
- Р. Йеошуа бен Леви говорит: если уста человека «дали плод» (*тнува*), ему возвещено, что молитва услышана. Основание — «בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם…» (Исайя 57:19).
- Отсюда обычное понимание: «знак» связан с тем, насколько молящийся собран и вовлечён. Ошибка в самом начале показывает, что внимания не хватает. Это понимание принадлежит комментаторам. Сам текст говорит лишь «дурной знак».
- Это именно *знак*, а не вердикт. Мишна не говорит, что молитва отвергнута, и не вводит наказания.

## Практически
Шулхан арух ([Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 101:1]) требует сосредоточиться во всех благословениях, а если не получается, то хотя бы в *Авот*. Там сказано, что без каваны в *Авот* нужно молиться заново. Рема добавляет, что сегодня из-за недостатка каваны не повторяют молитву, так как и при повторе, скорее всего, сосредоточиться не удастся.

Если вас интересует конкретный случай (например, вы сбились в Амиде), обратитесь к своему раввину.

answer:
Cette phrase vient de la Michna (*Mishna* Hagiga 2:1). Elle avertit que celui qui spécule sur ce qui est au-dessus, au-dessous, avant la création et après la fin du monde s'engage dans une recherche qui dépasse les limites de l'esprit humain. Elle concerne surtout la spéculation sans préparation sur la métaphysique et les mystères divins. Elle ne condamne pas la curiosité intellectuelle en général.

## Points clés

- La Michna dit : [Mishnah Chagigah 2:1] « כָּל הַמִּסְתַּכֵּל בְּאַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים, רָאוּי לוֹ כְּאִלּוּ לֹא בָּא לָעוֹלָם : מַה לְּמַעְלָה, מַה לְּמַטָּה, מַה לְּפָנִים, וּמַה לְּאָחוֹר ». Traduction : « Quiconque scrute quatre choses, il vaudrait mieux pour lui ne pas être venu au monde : ce qui est en haut, ce qui est en bas, ce qui est avant, ce qui est après. »
- Ces quatre choses sont : ce qui est au-dessus du firmament, ce qui est sous la terre, ce qui précédait la création, et ce qui suivra la fin du monde.
- La Guemara appuie cette limite sur un verset et sur Ben Sira : l'homme peut chercher à comprendre la création, mais pas ce qui est au-delà de ses bornes.
- Le Rambam y voit une mise en garde intellectuelle : celui qui spécule sur ces sujets sans formation ni méthode risque de tomber dans la confusion et l'erreur.
- La suite de la Michna, « celui qui ne ménage pas l'honneur de son Créateur », est expliquée de plusieurs façons.

## Le contexte dans la Michna

Cette phrase suit trois restrictions d'enseignement :
- on n'expose pas les arayot (unions interdites) devant trois personnes ;
- on n'expose pas le *Maassé Béréchit* (l'œuvre de la création) devant deux ;
- on n'expose pas le *Maassé Merkava* (le char divin d'Ézéchiel) devant un seul, sauf s'il est sage et comprend de lui-même.

Les quatre dimensions viennent ensuite, comme une limite plus générale encore.

## La source dans la Guemara

La Guemara ([Chagigah 11b]) tire cette limite d'un verset de Deutéronome 4:32 : « כִּי שְׁאַל נָא לְיָמִים רִאשֹׁנִים… וּלְמִקְצֵה הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד קְצֵה הַשָּׁמָיִם ». La Baraïta en déduit : « מִקְצֵה הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד קְצֵה הַשָּׁמַיִם אַתָּה שׁוֹאֵל, וְאֵין אַתָּה שׁוֹאֵל מָה לְמַעְלָה מָה לְמַטָּה, מָה לְפָנִים מָה לְאָחוֹר ». Traduction : « D'un bout du ciel à l'autre bout du ciel tu peux interroger, mais tu ne peux pas interroger sur ce qui est en haut, en bas, avant, après. »

Autrement dit, l'étude de la création telle qu'elle nous est donnée est permise, voire encouragée. Ce qui est interdit, c'est de chercher ce qui est hors de l'espace et du temps de la création.

La Guemara cite aussi Ben Sira ([Chagigah 13a]) : « בַּמּוּפְלָא מִמְּךָ אַל תִּדְרוֹשׁ, וּבַמְכוּסֶּה מִמְּךָ אַל תַּחְקוֹר. בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוֹרְשֵׁיתָ הִתְבּוֹנֵן, אֵין לְךָ עֵסֶק בַּנִּסְתָּרוֹת ». Traduction : « Ce qui est trop merveilleux pour toi, ne l'explore pas ; ce qui t'est caché, ne le sonde pas. Médite ce qui t'a été permis ; tu n'as pas à t'occuper des choses cachées. »

## L'explication du Rambam

Dans son commentaire sur la Michna ([Rambam on Mishnah Chagigah 2:1:1]), le Rambam propose une lecture rationaliste :
- Pour lui, *Maassé Béréchit* désigne la physique, la « sagesse naturelle ». *Maassé Merkava* désigne la métaphysique : l'existence de Dieu, les anges, l'âme, l'intellect.
- Ces sciences sont très élevées. Tout homme y pense naturellement, sage ou non. Mais celui qui s'y lance « sans introduction et sans degrés », c'est-à-dire sans avoir d'abord étudié les sciences préparatoires, risque de se tromper.
- Le Rambam explique la formule « il vaudrait mieux pour lui ne pas être venu au monde » ainsi : un tel homme, imaginant « en haut » et « en bas » comme une maison avec un étage, tombe dans « la folie et l'égarement du cœur ». Il vaudrait donc mieux pour lui n'être qu'un simple animal que d'abuser de l'intelligence humaine.
- Le Rambam précise que ces enseignements se transmettent de maître à élève, par tradition. La foule ne peut pas les comprendre, et un ignorant qui les entend voit sa foi troublée (voir aussi [Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 4:10]).

## « Celui qui ne ménage pas l'honneur de son Créateur »

La fin de la Michna dit : « וְכָל שֶׁלֹּא חָס עַל כְּבוֹד קוֹנוֹ, רָאוּי לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם ». Traduction : « Et quiconque ne ménage pas l'honneur de son Créateur, il vaudrait mieux pour lui ne pas être venu au monde. »

Le Rambam en propose deux lectures dans son commentaire :
- **L'honneur de Dieu est l'intellect humain.** Celui qui ne ménage pas son intelligence, en l'envoyant là où elle ne peut pas aller, ne ménage pas l'honneur de son Créateur.
- **Le péché en secret.** Il cite la lecture talmudique selon laquelle il s'agit de celui qui pèche en cachette, parce qu'il a moins de gêne devant Dieu que devant les hommes. Je n'ai pas pu vérifier ici le passage de la Guemara qui la contient. Je la rapporte donc d'après le Rambam et le *Yachin*.

Le commentaire *Yachin* relie les deux : celui qui s'interroge dans le secret sur ces mystères ne tient pas compte de l'honneur de Dieu.

## Que faut-il en retenir ?

- **Pas une interdiction de réfléchir.** Les Sages ont beaucoup étudié la création et le char divin, et la Guemara elle-même ([Chagigah 13a]) décrit les firmaments et les *Ḥayot*. La limite porte sur la manière et sur la préparation : seul un sage qui comprend par lui-même, ou un maître qui transmet des « têtes de chapitres » (*Roshé Perakim*), peut y entrer.
- **Les bornes de la connaissance humaine.** L'homme est créé dans le temps et l'espace. Chercher ce qui est avant le temps ou hors de l'espace revient à vouloir saisir ce qui par définition échappe à son entendement.
- **L'humilité.** Le sens est surtout moral : avoir « de la pitié pour l'honneur de son Créateur », c'est reconnaître ses limites devant Dieu.

Pour une application personnelle, par exemple savoir quoi étudier en kabbale ou en philosophie et avec quel guide, il vaut mieux consulter un rabbin ou un maître.

answer:
Kiddushin 32a is mostly about the details of honoring one's father: who pays for his food and drink, how far the son must go, and how to correct a father who is breaking a Torah law. It also discusses a father's and a teacher's power to waive their honor. The amud (page side) opens in the middle of a sugya (Talmudic discussion) and ends with Rava's reply to Rav Yosef. Here is a walkthrough; tell me if you'd rather have a line-by-line translation.

## Key Takeaways
- Practical halacha follows the view that a father's food and drink come from the father's own money if he has any. The son pays if the father has none.
- Even so, a son must give his time and effort, which may cost him income. This explains the verbal analogy to "Honor the Lord with your wealth".
- Rabbi Eliezer's limit for honor is that a son does not shame his father even if the father throws a purse into the sea.
- A son never says "you transgressed". He says, "Father, the Torah writes thus."
- A father may waive his honor. Rav Chisda says a teacher may not, but Rav Yosef says he may.

## 1. From whose money? (the opening)
The Mishnah says a son must feed and give his father drink. The Gemara asks: *mi-shel mi?* ("from whose money?").
- **Rav Yehuda:** from the son's money.
- **Rav Natan bar Oshaya:** from the father's money.
- The Sages ruled for Rav Yirmeya (some say for his son) like Rav Natan bar Oshaya: "כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר מִשֶּׁל אָב," meaning from the father's money.

The Gemara then tests this view against three sources:

1. **A baraita comparing honoring parents to "Honor the Lord with your wealth" (Proverbs 3:9).** It teaches that honoring a parent, like honoring God, involves "monetary loss" (*cheser kis*). If the money is the father's, what loss does the son suffer? The Gemara answers that he loses work time (*bitul melakhah*).
2. **A baraita on second tithe and poor man's tithe.** Father and son may feed each other poor man's tithe. If the son were obligated to support the father, he would be paying his own debt from the poor's property. The Gemara answers that this is only for *he'adafah*, a surplus beyond basic needs. Rabbi Yehuda nevertheless says: "תָּבֹא מְאֵירָה לְמִי שֶׁמַּאֲכִיל אֶת אָבִיו מַעְשַׂר עָנִי" ("a curse upon one who feeds his father poor man's tithe"). The Gemara explains this as *zila bei milta*, a degrading thing to do.
3. **Rabbi Eliezer: "How far does honor go?"** The answer is that the father takes the son's purse and throws it into the sea in front of him, and the son does not shame him. If the money were the father's, why would the son mind? The Gemara answers that this is a son who stands to inherit.

## 2. Rav Huna tears silk garments
Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabbah, saying he wanted to see whether Rabbah would get angry. The Gemara raises three problems and answers them:
- **"Before the blind do not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14).** Rav Huna was in effect tempting his son to sin by anger. The answer is that he had waived his honor (*machil li-yekareih*).
- **"Do not destroy" (*bal tashchit*).** The answer is that he did it publicly, in the *pumbeditha*-style gathering, as a test. In context, the act was done openly and was not wanton waste.
- **Maybe the son was not angry only because his father did it in a moment of anger.** The Gemara raises this as a possibility, so the test may prove nothing.

Ritva on Kiddushin 32a:1 asks a further question. The son does not know that his father has waived his honor, so how does the waiver help? He suggests that this prohibition, being a general "lav" (negative commandment), is not treated so strictly.

## 3. A digression: the Rav Yechezkel and Rami tangent
Rav Yechezkel taught his son Rami a ruling about those to be burned who got mixed in with those to be stoned. His other son, Rav Yehuda, objected to the formulation: if the majority are to be stoned, why give the reason that burning is more severe? He proposed reversing the wording. Rav Yechezkel replied that the reverse wording fails on the other half of the ruling, where the Sages say the group is judged by burning because stoning is more severe. Rashi explains that in that clause the Sages are not giving a reason. They are rejecting Rabbi Shimon's claim and ruling by the majority (Rashi on Kiddushin 32a:12:1).

This episode leads into the next point: Shmuel warns Rav Yehuda, called "Shinana", not to correct his father this way.

## 4. Correcting a father who violates the Torah
Shmuel quotes a baraita: a son whose father is violating a Torah law must not say, "אַבָּא עָבַרְתָּ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה" ("Father, you transgressed"). The Gemara asks whether even "so it is written in the Torah" causes him pain (*tza'ar*). It concludes that he says, "אַבָּא, מִקְרָא כָּתוּב בַּתּוֹרָה כָּךְ" ("Father, there is a verse in the Torah that reads this way"). The phrasing is posed as a question about the verse and does not accuse him.

## 5. When a father's request conflicts with a mitzvah
Elazar ben Matya says that if his father says "give me water" and a mitzvah needs doing, he lets his father's honor wait and does the mitzvah. His reasoning is that both he and his father are obligated in the mitzvah. Isi ben Yehuda says that if others can do the mitzvah, they should, and he should go and honor his father. Rav Matna rules like Isi ben Yehuda.

## 6. Waiving honor (*mechilah*)
- **Rav Chisda:** a father who waived his honor has waived it. A rabbi who waived his honor has not.
- **Rav Yosef:** even a rabbi's waiver is valid. Proof: "וַה׳ הֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵיהֶם יוֹמָם" ("and the Lord went before them by day," Exodus 13:21). God himself acted as a servant to Israel.
- **Rava rejects the proof:** "הָתָם, הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עָלְמָא דִּילֵיהּ הוּא, וְתוֹרָה דִּילֵיהּ הִיא" ("there the Holy One, blessed be He, the world is His and the Torah is His"). God can forgo His own honor, but a rabbi's honor belongs partly to the Torah. The discussion continues on 32b.

## Halachic bottom line
The Shulchan Arukh follows the ruling that the father pays if he can. If the father has nothing and the son has means, the court forces the son to support him as he can, but he need not go begging door to door [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 240:5]. The Rema adds a view that the son is obligated only to the extent he is obligated to give charity. Even so, "a curse comes upon one who supports his father from his charity money" if he can afford otherwise. The Shulchan Arukh also says the son must honor his father with his body even at cost of lost work income.

The Shulchan Arukh [Yoreh De'ah 240:25] also notes limits on a father's authority. A son need not obey his father's protest against a student's move to a place of better Torah study. The Rema adds that a son need not obey a father's objection to a marriage.

For a personal situation, consult your rabbi.

answer:
Let me try again.**Short answer:** Page 5 of Bava Metzia (Bava Metzia 5a and 5b) is about what a judge should do when two people say different things and nobody can be sure who is telling the truth. The Rabbis ask when someone has to promise ("swear") that he is telling the truth. They also ask when we can trust that promise. I used Sefaria's English translation as my base. The kid-friendly retelling is my own.

## Key Takeaways
- If a person says "I owe you some, but not all," the Torah makes him swear about the rest [Exodus 22:8].
- A shepherd who lied and ate some animals can't be trusted to swear, so the other side swears instead.
- When two people each hold half a cloak and both say "it's mine," each swears and they split it. This is a rule from the Rabbis to stop people from grabbing.
- A person who is only stalling for time is not the same as a robber.
- The Rabbis didn't treat everyone who does a wrong thing as a "bad guy." They looked at what the person was really thinking.

## The Big Idea for a 5-Year-Old

Imagine two kids at the playground. Dani says, "Yossi, I gave you 3 toy cars to hold, and you lost them!" Yossi says, "You only gave me 2, and one fell in a puddle by accident." A grown-up judge (a *dayan*) has to decide. The Torah has a special rule: if Yossi admits some of what Dani says but not all of it, he has to swear about the rest. The Torah's words are "for any lost item about which one shall say: This is it" [Exodus 22:8].

Page 5 is the Rabbis asking many "what if?" questions about that rule.

## Part 1 (5a): "Here you go!" and land

**Question: what if Yossi says, "Here, take back what I admit, and I never got the rest"?**
- Rav Sheshet says a person who just hands it back ("*hei lach*," "here you are") doesn't have to swear.
- The other side says he does have to swear.

**Land:** The Torah says there is no oath for land claims. Someone asks why the Torah needed to say that. Land never goes anywhere, so handing it back is always "here you are."

Rav Sheshet answers in two ways:
- Maybe the person dug holes and caves in the land, so it isn't the same as when he got it.
- Or someone claimed both tools and land, and the defendant admitted the tools but denied the land.

For a kid: a field can't run away. But if you dug big holes in your friend's sandbox, you can't just say "here it is" and be done.

**The cows:** The four kinds of guardians in the Torah are the unpaid watcher, the borrower, the paid watcher, and the renter. The Gemara says each of them swears only if he admits some of the claim and denies some. The example is three cows:
- "One cow? Never got it."
- "One died by accident."
- "One died because I wasn't careful. I'll pay for that one."

## Part 2 (5a): Witnesses

A baraita from Rabbi Aptoriki's father covers this case. Dani says "you owe me 100," Yossi says "nothing," and witnesses say Yossi really has 50.
- Should he swear about the other 50?
- Aptoriki's father says no. The verse says "*hu*" ("it") and "*zeh*" ("this"), so one word teaches that admitting part makes you swear, and the other teaches that witnesses' testimony does not.
- Rabbi Chiyya (the earlier one) learns something different from the same two words. His second lesson is that the admission has to be the same kind of item as the claim. The two sides also split on wheat versus barley, as in the Mishnah in Shevuot 38b, where Rabban Gamliel disagrees.

**The shepherd story:** A shepherd always got people's animals with witnesses watching. One day they gave him animals without witnesses, and he said, "I never got them." Then witnesses showed up and said he ate two. Rabbi Zeira says that if Rabbi Chiyya's rule is right, the shepherd should swear about the rest. Abaye objects: "He's a robber! Who would trust his oath?" Rabbi Zeira answers that he meant the other side swears and collects.

Even if the law isn't like Rabbi Chiyya, Rav Nachman made a rabbinic rule called the *shevuat heset* (oath of inducement). Under it, even a person who flatly says "I owe you nothing" gets asked to swear.

## Part 3 (5b): Can a shepherd's oath be trusted?

- The Gemara says "we don't build one rabbinic rule on top of another rabbinic rule," so a second rabbinic rule isn't added on top of Rav Nachman's.
- Rabbi Zeira could have just said "he's a shepherd, and shepherds are suspected of robbery" (Rav Yehuda says a regular shepherd is disqualified).
- The Gemara answers that this applies to a shepherd who grazes his own animals, because animals eat from other people's fields.
- A shepherd of other people's animals is different. Otherwise how could anyone hand their animals to a shepherd? That would put a stumbling block before the blind [Leviticus 19:14].
- The Gemara's reason: "a person sins only for his own benefit."

## Part 4 (5b): The cloak that two people grab

This comes back to the first Mishnah of the chapter, [Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1]. Two people grab one cloak and both say "it's all mine." Each swears that he owns at least half, and they divide it.

- **Why this wording?** Rav Huna says each says "I have a share in it, and not less than half." If he swore "it's all mine," the court wouldn't give him all of it. If he swore "half is mine," he would be weakening what he first claimed.
- **Why swear at all?** Each is already holding his part. Rabbi Yochanan says it is a rule of the Rabbis so that nobody goes and grabs someone else's cloak and says "it's mine."

## Part 5 (5b): "If he steals, he'd lie too, right?"

The Gemara asks: if someone is dishonest about money, shouldn't we assume he'd swear falsely too? It answers that we don't say that. Otherwise the person who admits part of the claim would also be a liar, and the Torah still makes him swear. That person is just stalling, as Rabba explains.

Evidence from Rav Chisda (quoted by Rav Idi bar Avin):
- Someone who denies a loan can still be a witness.
- Someone who denies a deposit can't, because he's holding something that isn't his.

The Gemara then explains why a guardian who says "I'll just pay" could still be trusted to swear. He may think, "I'll find the thief," or "I'll find it in the marsh." That is stalling, not stealing. The deposit-denier is disqualified only when witnesses say the item was in his house or hand while he denied it.

**The "don't want it" rule:** Rav Acha of Difti asks Ravina whether someone who pays for the item breaks the Torah rule "You shall not covet" [Exodus 20:14]. The answer is that ordinary people understand that rule to mean taking something without paying. So a person who pays can think he did nothing wrong, and his oath can still be believed.

## The Lesson in Kid Words
1. Tell the truth, even about small things.
2. Don't grab things that aren't yours.
3. If you "borrow" something, you are responsible for it.
4. Judges look at what's in a person's heart as well as what they did.
5. Someone who really means to keep something that isn't theirs is different from someone who is just scared and stalling.

answer:
Chullin 80a finishes the discussion of the *koy* (a creature of uncertain status, possibly part wild and part domesticated). It then begins the Gemara on Mishnah Chullin 5:1, which deals with *oto ve'et beno* (not slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day). I read most of the daf on Sefaria, but the lookups were rate-limited. I may have missed a line or two at the very end, and the Rabbi Oshaya passage below is cut off where my text stops.

## Key Takeaways
- Rav Pappa explains the koy rulings by applying the Rabbis' and Rabbi Eliezer's dispute over whether "sheep" includes a partial sheep.
- Amoraim and Tannaim dispute whether a koy is domesticated, wild, or its own category.
- Several Amoraim raise doubts about whether "Baala goats" are real goats fit for the altar.
- The daf then begins the Gemara on Mishnah 5:1, where Rabbi Oshaya says the mishna does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

## 1. Rav Pappa on the koy (continuing from 79b)
The Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer dispute how to read the word "שֶׂה" (sheep) in the verses. The Rabbis say it includes even a partial sheep. Rabbi Eliezer says it excludes a partial sheep.

Rav Pappa uses this to fit the koy rulings to the right cases.

- **Covering the blood and priestly gifts:** these apply only to a koy born of a **deer (male) mating with a she-goat**. Both sides are unsure whether we "worry about the father's seed." They differ on whether a partial sheep counts as a sheep. The Rabbis count it as domesticated for the gifts. Rabbi Eliezer exempts it.
- **Not slaughtering it and its offspring on one day:** this applies in either of two cases.
  - **A he-goat mating with a doe:** the Rabbis say it is **prohibited**, since we may worry about the father and "partial sheep" counts. There are no lashes, because the status is uncertain. Rabbi Eliezer says that even if we worry about the father, "partial sheep" does not count.
  - **A deer mating with a she-goat:** the Rabbis say it carries **lashes**. Rabbi Eliezer says it is prohibited but carries no lashes. It is prohibited because we might not worry about the father, which would make it a proper "sheep." It carries no lashes because we might worry about the father, and then a partial sheep does not count.

## 2. What is a koy? (the dispute)
- **Rav Yehudah:** it is a creature in its own right, and the Sages did not decide whether it is a domesticated or a wild species.
- **Rav Nachman:** it is a wild ram (*ayil habar*).
- The Gemara links this to a baraita, quoted at [Chullin 80a:12]:
  - **First view:** a wild ram.
  - **"Some say":** the offspring of a goat and a deer.
  - **Rabbi Yosei:** a distinct creature, status undecided.
  - **Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel:** a domesticated species. The house of Dushai raised flocks of them.

## 3. "Baala goats" and the altar
Rav Hamnuna (as relayed by Rabbi Zeira and Rav Safra) says these goats are fit for the altar. His reasoning follows Rabbi Yitzchak: the Torah lists only ten *behemot* (domesticated animals), and these are not counted among the *chayot* (wild animals). So they must be goats.

- **Rav Acha bar Yaakov** objects. The verse says "ayal and tzvi" (a specific list) and then "kol behemah" (a general term). A specific-then-general list adds to the general category, so there are many more domesticated animals. The Gemara asks why the verse then lists all the specifics, and leaves that as a difficulty.
- **Rav Acha son of Rav Ika:** perhaps they are a type of *akko* (wild goat).
- **Rav Acha son of Rava, or of Rav Avya, to Rav Ashi:** perhaps they are a type of *te'o* (aurochs) or *zemer* (wild sheep).
- **Rav Chanan to Rav Ashi:** Ameimar permitted their fat. That treats them as wild, since the fat of domesticated animals is forbidden.
- **Abba son of Rav Minyamin bar Chiya asks Rav Huna bar Chiya.** Rav Huna says Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis disagree only about the wild ox (*shor habar*). The Rabbis call it domesticated because it is translated *torbala*. Rabbi Yosei calls it wild because it is listed with the *chayot*. About these goats, everyone agrees they are a type of goat. The same objections are raised again, with Ravina and Rav Nachman in the roles of the earlier questioners.

## 4. New section: the mishna on "oto ve'et beno"
The Gemara now turns to [Mishnah Chullin 5:1]. That mishna covers the Leviticus 22:28 prohibition ("You shall not slaughter it and its offspring both in one day"). It says the prohibition applies:
- in Israel and abroad,
- in Temple times and after,
- to both non-sacred and sacrificial animals.

It then gives four cases.
- **Non-sacred animals slaughtered outside:** both are valid, and the second slaughterer gets lashes.
- **Sacrificial animals slaughtered outside:** the first slaughterer is liable to *karet* (excision). Both animals are disqualified, and both slaughterers get lashes.
- **Non-sacred animals slaughtered inside:** both are disqualified, and the second slaughterer gets lashes.
- **Sacrificial animals slaughtered inside:** the first is valid and its slaughterer is exempt. The second is disqualified and its slaughterer gets lashes.

**Rabbi Oshaya** says the entire mishna does not follow **Rabbi Shimon**. His proof is the second case, where the mishna says both slaughterers get lashes. Rabbi Shimon holds that "slaughter that is not fit [to permit the meat] is not called slaughter," and the Gemara begins to build on that.
